Every major breakthrough in artificial intelligence is matched by significant setbacks. Although these stumbles in AI development seem to plateau in the realm of chess and go, similar patterns of rise and fall also occur in initiatives to understand human brains, achieve general intelligence, and applications in vision, hearing, speech, drug discovery, language, ethics, and more. Instead of getting stuck in this cycle, researchers have started exploring innovative solutions. One such idea, termed the AI Incident Repository, involves systematically collecting and organizing AI setbacks across various domains and levels of technology maturity, facilitating an evidence-based analysis of past mistakes and fostering collaborative problem-solving within the AI community. By making this repository publicly accessible, more robust and accountable AI systems can be created.

Our precise renormalization group (PRGR) method enables the numerical solution of the renormalization group flow with high precision for a broad class of problems. The PRGR approach combines gradient descent and a novel time-reparameterization technique to overcome limitations of the renormalization group equation, making it a differential equation that can be solved with standard methods. We have applied PRGR to various problems, including finding fixed points of the O(N) model in up to N=4 dimensions, determining critical exponents for the Fisher-Kolmogorov-Pereziam equation, and providing a fixed-point action for QFT in a given irreducible representation of the diffeomorphism group in two-dimensional gravity. Our framework is versatile and can be applied to any problem involving renormalization group equations.

Human interaction specifications often require capturing both intentional and unintentional aspects of human behavior. While many researchers have incorporated this requirement into models of human interactions, many are trained to overlook violations of unintentional specifications due to human errors. However, most existing approaches focus on detecting discrepancies between actual human behavior and intended behaviors after they occur. To proactively prevent and resolve human system disputes, we need a method for monitoring real-time human behavior and identifying potential violations between intentional and unintentional specifications as they happen. In this research, we introduce a new method using automata theory to monitor real-time human behavior and prevent disputes by identifying potential violations in real-time human behavior and offering timely warnings to users.

We define a formal theoretical framework, called a machine model, to examine the behavior and properties of a quantum programming language, known as Proto-Quipper-M. Our work adapts and builds upon existing machine model definitions, modifying them to accurately represent the characteristics of a quantum programming language. Instead of relying on word-level representations, we modify our model to use a representation method suited for quantum programs, making it easier to analyze program equivalence and facilitate the development of verification tools. Additionally, we demonstrate that an adapted machine model is both complete and reliable by proving that the two are semantically equivalent.

We're investigating a family of random matrices derived from the real and complex Gaussian ensembles by applying a real polynomial of a high degree to their eigenvalues. When doing so, the distribution of the extreme eigenvalues of these ensembles is significantly altered, leading to a scaling behavior that differs from the standard universal profiles. Notably, the average spacing between the extreme eigenvalues changes from a power-law to a more nuanced, non-trivial function of the parameter. This space is also separated into distinct domains, with the boundary defined by a delicate balance between large and small fluctuations of the parameter. In contrast, the universal profiles of the extreme eigenvalues remain unchanged within each of these separate domains, while also exhibiting reflection symmetry. Furthermore, at the boundary between these domains, the parameters of the extreme eigenvalues evolve in a continuous manner, ultimately giving rise to a new, distinct universal profile at the point where the two domains converge.

A proposed method to create pairs of bosonic particles in mass using a cavity of light involves having it interact with two two-state systems or dipoles. It's specifically investigated here as to how a pair in mass can lead to a type of compression of light, which may be assessed using the Bell inequality to break through a certain ceiling set by the system's complexity. According to a simplified model in which the system is at rest and the dipole interaction is instant, it appears that a high level of compression is possible under specific conditions. These conditions involve setting the dipole interaction strength in relation to a parameter that controls how quickly the system loses energy to the environment through the cavity walls. It's found that even significant energy loss can result in a measurable level of compression using an appropriate choice of parameters, which can lead to precise measurements in the relationship between the phase of light and something else.

As a crucial step in genome assembly, aligning read reads to build a de novo genome assembly is crucial but poses computational challenges due to its massive data requirements. Parallel computing has effectively addressed this challenge by significantly reducing the time needed to align reads through all-reduce operations. However, this approach is hindered in large-scale simulations due to the high communication overhead associated with the global all-reduce operation. To address this limitation, a new fully distributed-memory parallel creation method has been developed to align read reads more efficiently, thus reducing communication costs. This optimized approach employs a custom data structure that organizes reads in a contiguous format and utilizes the locality of the data to minimize communication. As a result, the optimized data structure allows for the alignment of all reads with just one local access, thus eliminating the need for a global all-reduce operation. This optimized data structure has been integrated into a fast and efficient de novo long-read genome assembly software to facilitate the distributed-memory parallel assembly of large genomes. This innovative approach has demonstrated favorable outcomes on a set of 20 test datasets, producing highly accurate and complete genome assemblies even in the face of massive data volumes. This optimized data structure can be applied to other massive data processes that were previously limited by communication costs, thus enabling the efficient processing of massive data.

A modified logistic equation, previously studied in a previous work, has been further investigated in this study. The researchers further simplified the equation into a simpler form and used analytical and graphical methods to examine its positive solutions, providing further insight into its global behavior.

The traditional regression depth extends the concept of multivariate median to dependent (y, x) data and offers various properties for statistical hypothesis testing and ranking. Unfortunately, effective computational methods are limited to y | x Gaussian data with y | x t-distribution alternatives. We expand upon the depth concept by introducing a new approach based on pointwise stochastic orders and propose a novel transformation, the Isometric Log-Change Transformation (ILTC), that enables classical probability tools to be applied to Rank dependence structures. We then define a new nonparametric depth for pointwise data (y, x) using a concept derived from stochastic dominance and corresponding statistical distance metrics. This new depth is computationally efficient and includes an index that measures how well a pointy, x) ranks relative to the data cloud. We utilize bootstrap resampling to calculate p-values and confidence sets for testing statistical hypotheses. Two case studies illustrate our approach's effectiveness in analyzing real data sets.

We develop a theoretical model for a perfect superconducting hybrid device,
composed of a 1D spin-charge entangled carrier system coupled to a BCS
superconductor, and design a planar ideal quantum circuit to study and examine
the underlying non-Abelian order and designed quantum states of spin-charge
entangled carriers. Our analysis employs both microscopic and low-energy
effective descriptions and utilizes both descriptions to address key issues,
including the nature of the unique quantum state formed through their
association with the superconductor, the non-Abelian order of the carriers,
the entanglement within the spin subsystem, and the entanglement among the
charged components. We also investigate the stability of the unique quantum
state and its non-Abelian order via Rashba interaction, magnetic impurities,
long-range Coulomb interaction, and electric fields. Moreover, the entanglement
within the spin and charged components is thoroughly studied by means of
dynamical structure factors and entanglement spectrum analysis. Our findings
are substantiated by employing an exact diagonalization approach and by
demonstrating that the entanglement spectrum accurately reproduces low-lying
excitations. Finally, the non-Abelian order of the carriers is experimentally
validated using dynamical tunneling spectroscopy and by substantiating dynamic
stability against a hypothetical topological disorder.

Researchers employed two advanced atomic spectrometry techniques, specifically laser spectroscopy with a laser-cooled magneto-optical trap and radio-frequency quadrupole mass spectrometry, to accurately measure the atomic mass of six Germane isotopes, to = $^{70,72,74}$Ge, in an effort to minimize atomic structure information to atomic mass data. By integrating this work with prior studies on Germane isotopes, they were able to refine the atomic mass values to the precision of $10^{-11}$ to $10^{-12}$ relative to $^{40}$Ca, matching the high-precision standards of nuclear physics. Moreover, they were able to quantify the isotopic shift in Germane, characterizing it to the precision of $10^{-10}$ relative to $^{70}$Ge, and this contributed to an update of the atomic shell model in an extreme way towards the neutron drip line.

The development of a precise and efficient isochronous mass spectrometry technique relies heavily on the accurate determination of the product of the magnetic field and orbital radius (Bρ) for charged ions. Research has shown that high-precision mass measurements can be achieved, reaching a precision of 2.5 ppm in a related experiment. A new method was developed to accurately calculate Bρ for highly charged, short-lived nuclei. This method involved the precise measurement of the revolution times of these nuclei and their singly charged daughter products using a specialized detector. A key component in calculating Bρ was the radius of a 0.5 T dipole magnet's orbit within a 3D-Track chamber, determined through a thorough analysis of tracking efficiency and the precise positioning of the detector's center. A thorough study was also conducted to minimize the influence of the relativistic mass of the nuclei and to accurately locate the dipole magnet's aperture. As a proof of concept, a precise mass measurement of a 20Ne ion was carried out, demonstrating a precision of 2.5 ppm. This research demonstrates that a precise Bρ calculation for short-lived nuclei is feasible through an accurate tracking system, thereby enabling the application of ischroous mass spectrometry to unstable nuclei with very short lifetimes.

This brief overview showcases the technique of using modified flows to determine field theory lattice actions that are standardised. It specifically relies on the framework of modified flow equations first developed in arXiv:1308.2671, which has been designed to accurately reproduce physical characteristics of field theories when discretised. The text also discusses the concepts of lattice actions that are standardised and how they can be determined using modified flow trajectories. Additionally, it explores the possibilities of applying this method to improve reannangement techniques, determine lattice actions from theoretical models, and potentially leading to the development of new flow-based Monte Carlo methods.

Identifying unlabelled structured text such as emails and invoices presents significant challenges due to high variability in wording and layout. Our approach utilizes deep learning-based optical character recognition and feature-engineered content to achieve this, specifically using a novel network called IDNet for text recognition and refined character-level features including invariance to regular expressions, leading to improved accuracy and production-ready performance on a public dataset.

A model is proposed to check for top quark production in proton-nucleus collisions.
Using this model, we calculate cross-sections for specific energy and mass ranges,
and compare them to results from simulations in pythia 8.4 for both 33 and 92 GeV beam energies.
Our findings show that the models are consistent for 33 GeV, but deviate for 92 GeV,
implying the models may complement each other in studying high-energy interactions.
Key differences exist in the proton-nucleon and nucleus-proton interactions at 92 GeV,
notably in top quark differential distributions, suggesting these interactions are distinct.

This research focuses on addressing the cross-domain text-to-SQL conversion problem, which involves translating user queries into SQL statements across different database domains. The proposed solution employs a two-stage framework, beginning with a user query analysis module that converts the question into semantic representations, including entity identification, relational information, and operational context, all of which are then used in the SQL generation stage. The derived semantic information guides the SQL generator in formulating accurate and relevant statements. The framework was implemented using Transformer models for both stages and extensively tested on multiple database domains to evaluate its utility in improving cross-domain text-to-SQL conversion.

A comprehensive radio survey, known as the LOFAR Two-metre Sky Survey (proto-DATA RELEASE 1), covers nearly 5000 square degrees of the sky in the continuum band from 110 to 164 MHz. This survey is divided into four distinct fields: the Bright Arcfield, Croton et al 2002 North Field 2, Deep North Field 1, and Deep South Field 1. This paper focuses on the radio properties of galaxies within the Bright Arcfield, the Deep North Field 1, and the Deep South Field 1. Radio flux densities were determined for a comprehensive sample of 10,743 galaxies, covering a wide range of absolute magnitudes and redshifts. Additionally, the relationship between radio and optical flux, as well as the connection between r1500 and absolute magnitude, was found to follow a clear trend, which then plateaus for brighter galaxies. This study also reveals a distinct change in the galaxy energy spectrum at an absolute magnitude of approximately -18.5. Furthermore, the galaxy bias as a function of absolute magnitude was found to follow a clear pattern, indicating that brighter galaxies are more biased. This is in line with other findings in the literature, but the rate at which bias increases for brighter galaxies was found to be slightly lower.

The high-dimensional rank LASSO problem, a key component in various statistical analysis methods, poses significant computational difficulties due to its non-convex and non-differentiable nature. Existing algorithms struggle to efficiently solve large-scale instances, particularly those involving regression metrics like Tjur distance and correlation, which are commonly used in analytical workflows but pose optimization challenges. To overcome these limitations, we developed an innovative, adaptive-sifting-based algorithm called ASO, which effectively addresses the Tjur and correlation metrics by incorporating two key mechanisms. First, we integrated a generalized coordinate descent approach with coordinate selection, which focuses on a limited number of key variables and eliminates redundant ones. Second, we developed an efficient update rule that leverages variable sparsity and reduces the algorithmic update complexity to linear time, allowing for rapid convergence even in large-scale datasets exceeding a million rows. Through extensive experimentation, ASO demonstrated substantial improvements over current methods, achieving up to tenfold decreases in convergence iterations and achieving unprecedented performance gains in terms of convergence speed and test errors on various Tjur and correlation maximization/minimization instances.

As knowledge of large-scale systems grows, understanding of irreversible processes has been limited to the thermodynamics of small systems, due to a lack of relevant examples in engineering applications. We have developed rapid and efficient methods for creating entropy in ideal gases through'shake and tilt'protocols, enabling a thorough thermodynamic analysis. We present analytical solutions for driving protocols that are suitable for implementation in experiments, and find that they yield predictable thermodynamic behavior, with the following key findings: (a) in the limit of swift motion, the entropy generated is equivalent to that of small systems, and (b) in the limit of gradual driving, the entropy generated is proportional to the entropy change, with a convex relationship that is influenced by the system's initial state, and an exponential dependency on the non-linearity of the interaction. These findings suggest that it is feasible to create entropy in large systems with disorder and to generate entropy with minimal influence from the system's initial conditions.

This paper explores the hidden environmental impacts of using AI in information and communication technologies (ICT) through life cycle assessment (LCA). To fill the LCA database gaps for AI models, we conducted four separate surveys to gather production data, analyzing the ecological consequences of specific AI types such as computer vision and large language models. The results reveal significant differences in the embodied energy and non-renewable energy carrier consumption between complex AI models and simpler ones, highlighting the need for more sustainable AI designs. Furthermore, our analysis fills a research void by providing the first LCA-based evaluation of AI's environmental effects in ICT, thus filling a critical gap in existing studies.

Research in prescriptive procedure monitoring has been expanding over the last two decades, focusing on real-time process adjustments to achieve optimal business process outcomes. A significant yet under-researched aspect within this field is adjusting timelines, yet our current understanding of timeline adjustments is fragmented across various studies, each addressing unique scenarios. This study provides an overview of existing prescriptive timeline adjustment research, categorizing them based on underlying assumptions and evaluation methodologies, before proposing a classification framework for future research. This framework, illustrated with examples, can serve as a guide for future investigations into prescriptive procedure monitoring.

This study develops an a posteriori error indicator to regulate discretization errors in simulations of a heat-sensitive material using a generalized Boussinesq model. The primary objective is to maintain the stability and accuracy of numerical solutions, particularly in capturing key processes such as natural convection patterns and phase transitions. We modify a previously proposed a posteriori analysis by incorporating elements specific to heat transfer and a nonlinear constitutive model. The resulting error indicator accounts for the influence of a variable density field and non-linear stress-strain relationships on various numerical approximations. Through numerical experiments, including a test on a heated square domain and a simulation of solidification in a circular domain, we demonstrate that utilizing mesh refinement driven by the proposed error indicator leads to solutions with final errors comparable to those achieved with significantly finer uniform meshes.

Machine learning, a core area of computer science, is expanding with novel applications and theoretical contributions. One significant apportionment within this domain involves stacking models, which are evaluated based on their predictive capabilities. In response to the increased significance of stacking models, we address the computational complexity of two stack construction problems, focusing on their membership to the NP-complete category. Furthermore, we develop polynomial-time kernelization techniques for these problems, key findings of which are deeply rooted in the underlying theory and difficult to articulate simply, making them particularly challenging to grasp.

The study revolves around the notion of limited but enhanced confidence in cointegration by examining the interplay between increased reliance and perspectives within the framework of a shift in emphasis. This investigation of structural assurance involves determining the relationship between possible structural configurations and various views, all while maintaining consistency in the increased reliance and perspectives system, which has been found to be intimately tied to the theoretical concept of rational uncertainty. The theoretical concept of a preference for particular combinations is used to describe the inherent inclination towards certain structural configurations, all while maintaining consistency with the theoretical concept of a preference for particular combinations. The increased reliance and perspectives system, all determined through the theoretical concept of a preference for particular combinations, results in an inclination towards certain structural configurations, all while maintaining consistency with the theoretical concept of a preference for particular combinations. Inside a fuzzy star, we develop a new spherically symmetric model to represent matter with intrinsic fuzziness, and derive the associated fuzzy Tolman-Oppenheimer-Volkoff equations. By investigating the transition from fuzzy to classical matter, we identify three distinct possibilities. Within a certain range of parameters, we succeed in solving the fuzzy equations both at infinity and at the center, and examine the properties of the resulting fuzzy black hole solutions, including their interior, event horizon, and singularity. Our analysis also features a fuzzy version of the ISCO for rotating stars.

Recent research has brought our understanding of gene expression regulation a step closer, thanks to advances in modeling that cover an entire genome. However, current modeling methods often oversimplify a crucial aspect: the time difference, or lag, between mRNA and protein production. Our findings from analyzing a comprehensive genome of yeast demonstrate that, under normal and stressful conditions, the behavior of proteins cannot be fully predicted by looking at the base levels of mRNA, but rather by understanding its temporal fluctuations, which are influenced by various factors, including chromosomal location and the precise position of genes within the nucleus. These discoveries emphasize the significance of considering RNA production dynamics when studying gene regulation and the value of incorporating improved modeling of transient mRNA patterns into our models of protein production.

The in-depth analysis of six nucleon units beyond the closed shell in $^{64}$Ni, particularly its null spin states, is guided by findings from studies on the $^{60}$Ni, $^{62}$Ni and $^{64}$Ni low-lying states. The investigation centers on the form coexistence characteristic of this nucleus, where two distinct types of minormajor shell model configurations interact. By applying the constrained antisymmetrized generator coordinate method, we've evaluated how a specific component of the nuclear force, the Wigner force represented by $Q_{TM=0}^{(6)}$, impacts three-minor and six-nucleon unit models of $^{64}$Ni, demonstrating that $^{64}$Ni's form coexistence can be accounted for through this interaction alone, without incorporating pairing. Furthermore, our study predicted $^{64}$Ni's mid-spin states, exhibiting good agreement with experimental data.

Chiral SU(N) theories, particularly for odd values of N and S, exhibit an anomaly that cannot be resolved supersymmetrically, resulting in a non-zero result. We suggest that a variant of the SU(N) super-Yang-Mills theory, using N+1 supersymmetry, and an additional chiral matter field set, X, Y, could potentially be in dual equilibrium with the chiral SU(N) theory, using S matter fields. Our hypothesis is supported by several key points: the S value matches the S value in the variant; the gauge symmetry is the same in both theories; matter zero modes are the same in both theories; the 't Hooft anomaly is the same in both theories; and N=2 supersymmetric subsets within the theories are in dual equilibrium, according to the N=4 duality in the N=2 theory, and the confinement and no-symmetry result in the N+1 set, containing the field set X, Y.

A linear complementary set of group codes (LCGC) over a finite principal ideal domain $D$ and a finite abelian group $G$ comprises a collection of group subcodes $\{C_i\}_{i = 1}^s$, where each $C_i$ corresponds to a subgroup of $D^n$ and their direct sum equals $D^n$. A survey of existing research into LGCGs is presented, and a novel framework for analyzing subcodes of group codes from the perspective of ideal transforms in the group ring $D[G]$ is provided. Utilizing the concept of ideal transforms, distinct definitions of LGCGs are presented, and various equivalent characterizations are established based on this theory. Moreover, the application of LGCGs to constructing complementary subspaces in $D^n$ via a single subcode is considered, and the conditions for achieving this construction are given using both ideal transforms and Wu's character method. The application of LGCGs to three specific cases, namely $D = \mathbb{F}_q[T]/(f)$, $D = \mathbb{F}_q[G_0]$ and $D = \mathbb{F}_q[S_3]$, where $G_0$ is a cyclic group and $S_3$ is the symmetric group on three letters, leads to novel results and characterizations.

Recently, there's been a shift towards using neural networks, but this often leads to
optimization difficulties, including issues with finding global optima, overfitting,
and neccessity for large datasets. A key benefit of traditional machine learning
algorithms is their ability to theoretically guarantee finding optima, and when
these algorithms can be combined with the expressive power of neural networks,
there's potential for overcoming their limitations. In this paper, we aim to
explore Faster Elimination for Maximum Expected Payoff, a recent technique that
exactly optimizes Markov Decision Processes with multiple agent decisions and no
cycles in their interaction graphs. We will also consider a functional approach
to representation, specifically using additive and compositional functions, to
facilitate FEA's application to a wider range of MDE problems.

We investigate the issue of identifying items susceptible to confusion through their names and images, which is crucial in various applications such as multi-modal retrieval, language-based image search, and robust visual recognition. To address this challenge, we develop a novel approach that asynchronously fuses audio-visual data to detect anomalies. The method involves a basic model with separate image and audio encoders, a contrastive learning module and a binary classifier that are end-to-end trainable. An exception discriminator is employed to identify prone cases, which are gradually introduced to improve model robustness. The method's efficacy is demonstrated through quantitative and qualitative experiments on two benchmark datasets, showcasing its state-of-the-art performance in fusing asynchronous audio-visual data for detecting items prone to confusion.

To investigate the role of shear in influencing self-organized critical systems, we studied a simplified version of theavalanche model that incorporates a parameter (quench rate) to introduce global non-equilibrium conditions. Our non-equilibrium system exhibits a single critical point, and we found that at this point there is an interesting interplay between shear and non-equilibrium quenching rate. Additionally, we observed that the non-equilibrium quenching rate gives rise to two distinct regimes of behavior, and within one of these regimes there is an interesting connection to systems in equilibrium under the influence of shear. Our study also provides a basic framework for understanding the complex interactions between shear and non-equilibrium effects and how they influence self-organized critical systems.

This research paper outlines a mathematical model for analyzing electricity consumption patterns on an hourly basis during periods of power shortage. We provide and apply computer code in Excel and MATLAB to solve the model and generate illustrative graphs of electricity usage for various days within the power crisis period.

This research provides empirical evidence on the scope of information that users may inadvertently overlook as a result of customizing Google Web Search, due to how the most pertinent and visually appealing results are prioritized. Participants who had previously customized their Google search to prioritize high-ranking results were less inclined to engage with results that appeared lower in the customized search order, yet remained pertinent to their queries, compared to those using the default search without customization. This study emphasizes the importance of how users interact with Search Engine Results Pages (SERPs) and the influence of their personal customization on their ability to access all relevant information, underscoring the need for further investigation into the potential impact of their personalization on their information seeking behavior.

Recent advances in machine learning, particularly in neural networks, have led to the development of applications in diagram-based learning tasks. However, recent approaches are limited to recognizing basic diagrams and have not been tested on more complex diagrams with multiple entities and relationships. To address this limitation, we introduce a novel deep learning approach, Graph Recognition ConvNets (GRCNN), which uses Convolutional Neural Networks to recognize complex graphs directly from static images without the need for coordinate-based encoding. Our model employs a novel encoding technique and can effectively distinguish between various graphs representing flow processes. Experiments demonstrate the feasibility of end-to-end training of GRCNN and its potential to generate correct programs from graphs directly, given that a template-based code generator is applied to its output.

This detailed technical note outlines the mathematical foundation of climate models of varying complexity - atmospheric, oceanic, and their interactions - and their global and local average climates. It also explores the atmospheric model's global and local average climates using contraction theory, which encompasses metrical regularity, average absolute difference, and ergodic theory approaches. These theories include ergodicity, Lyapunov functions, and absolute differences, providing a more comprehensive theory of climate existence and uniqueness. Notably, this mathematical framework for climate models is both rigorous and accessible to experts in atmospheric and oceanic modeling as well as mathematicians and mathematicians of moderate specialization.

A detailed calculation has been carried out on the energy levels and transition probabilities for the $5d^6 6s$ low-lying electron configuration of Au IV and related ions, particularly in a range of temperatures and densities relevant to kilonova ejecta. For ions with the $5d^6 6s$ ground state, our data significantly deviates from existing sources, whereas our results partially match a older dataset. Conversely, for ions with the $5d^7$ ground state, our calculated transition probabilities are lower than those in existing databases. A comparative study on the $5d^8 6s$ low-lying electron configuration of Au V and related ions has been conducted. In ejecta with $Z/A \approx 0.7$, our results indicate that opacity due to $6s$-involving transitions is comparable to that caused by a rare earth element, whereas in ejecta with a higher $Z/A$, this ratio becomes disproportionately high.

Radiological diagnosis accuracy heavily relies on precise image segmentation, which is often hindered by the complexity of medical images. The images' heterogeneity and noise pose significant challenges for traditional segmentation methods, which rely on handcrafted features and rules. These methods are time-consuming and require expert knowledge, making them impractical for clinical settings. The advent of deep learning, which automatically extracts relevant information from data, has opened new possibilities for image segmentation. This study presents an advanced deep learning-based approach for segmenting anatomical structures within pig livers and guts, addressing the difficulties associated with multiple, irregular gastrointestinal structures. Our methodology employs a U-Net architecture for image segmentation and utilizes optimized stochastic gradient descent with momentum for training the convolutional neural network. To enhance feature extraction and overcome challenges associated with small structures and class imbalance, we applied data augmentation and a loss function optimized for this purpose. Our model's performance is superior to existing state-of-the-art models, as evidenced by a 97% average dice coefficient for pig liver and gut automated segmentation.

Compositional data, characterized by interdependent variables constrained by a fixed sum, often presents itself in the forms of percentages, proportions, or ratios. Due to these constraints, classical statistical methods can produce spurious correlations and inaccurate conclusions. A compositional data examination is proposed as a systematic approach to investigate compositional data using linear algebra and visualization techniques, enabling researchers to understand the data's structure and dependencies more effectively.

No planets similar to Saturn have been discovered within their respective stellar systems through the CORALIE/HARPS survey, and our comprehensive search of these detections (93 confirmed systems, ranging from 5.5 to 80 Earth masses) has yielded novel insights. We analyzed the distribution of masses and orbital periods for these planets and found that those with masses between 5.5 and 15 Saturn masses tend to have shorter orbital periods of less than 200 days. Furthermore, we examined the effects of detection biases and found that the desert of Sub-Saturn mass planets may actually be an inherent feature of radial velocity exoplanets, rather than the result of atmospheric evaporation. In support of this notion, we observed that smaller exoplanets tend to have longer orbital periods than those with masses similar to Saturn, and we found that systems with masses between 15 Saturn masses and those with masses greater than 30 Earth masses share a desert of long orbital periods, which may be attributed to tidal interactions.

Gathering sufficient, high-quality knowledge from diverse mutual sources is a crucial factor in advancing mutual knowledge. To efficiently collect and share knowledge, we have developed a novel regulation strategy called TATR (Tough Attention Regulation). By incorporating a structured attention mechanism that enhances and propagates knowledge from various directions, TATR facilitates a thorough exploration and aggregation of all input data under rigorous attention checks, leading to a significant提升 in network performance and output robustness and efficiency. Experimental results using multiple benchmark datasets confirm the effectiveness of our approach and its ability to surpass existing state-of-the-art models. The open-source code has been made available on GitHub for educational and research purposes at https://github.com/chenyuxu99/TATR.

If dark matter is composed of sub-proton mass particles that interact via a Yukawa force mediated by a dark photon, the clumpy nature of these particles' distribution can be enhanced. The Yucawa potential's long-range, exponentially-interacting nature leads to the clustering of dark matter at both galactic and sub-galactic scales. The strength and range of this interaction are influenced by the dark photon's coupling and mass. The Yukawa force's effect on the halos of galaxies and galaxy clusters can be modeled and compared to cold dark matter models. In some cases, this clumpiness is maximized, potentially leading to elevated indirect detection rates in regions with lower densities. This clumpiness is most pronounced in certain parameter ranges, but could also be present outside of the commonly explored areas. These maximally-clumped dark matter configurations are characterized by a unique, localized, and dynamic nature, differing significantly from the assumed cold and smooth dark matter. This new understanding of clumped dark matter is explored in detail, considering its implications for the galactic halo's density fluctuations and substructure.

In recent years, recurrent neural networks (RNNs) have gained significant traction in the study of cognitive modeling. To tackle complex tasks, such as the 8-N-SAT problem, most successful cNN models have been over-parametrized, requiring extensive training data and search spaces. To address this limitation, we propose a novel learning rule that leverages sparse recurrent neural networks to simulate neurobiological learning mechanisms. By incorporating biologically plausible constraints, such as fixed architectures and negative Hebbian weight clipping, we can achieve rapid convergence in the fraction of correct trials within a fraction of the training iterations needed by standard gradient methods. This approach not only enables our models to attain high performance levels in the 8-N-SAT problem but also generalizes its solution to 6-SAT and 7-SAT variants, all of which exhibit similar quick learning patterns. Furthermore, our computational results suggest a potential link between neural sparsity and task complexity, with more complex tasks demanding sparser neural representations. This model's ability to produce task-dependent neural representations makes it suitable for future applications in neural-cognitive systems that need to solve a variety of cognitive tasks efficiently.

This work delves into a specific type of nilpotent algebra by examining its associations with the cohomology of associative algebras. To that end, a collection of equivalences has been established, allowing for the comparison of two geometric characteristics. Furthermore, a standard measure for nilpotency has been defined based on this understanding. The work also introduces various algebraic structures and provides concrete examples to illustrate the applied theory.

At the highest redshifts, galaxies form and activate massive black holes, producing jets of active galactic nuclei (AGN). These jet particles, moving through the surrounding intergalactic medium, generate magnetohydrodynamic waves, causing the gas to become magnetized and amplify its field through instability. This process can lead to the generation of higher energy stars, making the effect of amplification crucial to understand in relation to the background of the cosmic microwave radiation. This is because the effect of the acceleration of the particles is limited by the condition that the energy they gain is less than the energy in the CMB photons, limiting the redshift beyond which the effect of the acceleration is severely restricted. This paper calculates, using numerical simulations, how the evolution of the temperature and density of the gas is limited by the effect of the temperature and density fluctuations in the CMB, and how this impacts the application of the maximum redshift limit to this process. We have discovered that in the case of the aggregation of the gas by the effect of the cosmic structure, the maximum redshift limit is still applicable, however, the effect of the temperature and density fluctuations in the CMB can significantly raise this limit, up to 6 for a temperature fluctuation of 10 percent and a particle to photon ratio of $10^5$.

This section provides concise definitions of various Lagrangians commonly used in classical gravity theories. It also examines the implications of absolute Lorentz invariance and analyzes why, despite being well-behaved, the identified Lagrangians are ineffective in theoretical and experimental physics.

Our image registration approach  handles the specific characteristics of picture-based data, like 3D scans of teeth. image alignment using a 3D model and a corresponding image is accomplished by first extracting keypoints from both the image and 3D data. image transformation data, collected from a CT scan, is used to map the 3D point cloud to the desired view, allowing for the calculation of corresponding 2D points in the image, which can then be used to determine similarity and generate a transformation matrix. this approach's efficacy, compared to an alternative method, was assessed through the alignment of dental image pairs, with results showing that our strategy provides more accurate results, especially at higher image similarity levels.

Our 2009-2017 photometric study of DDO 444945, an approximately 40.5-minute orbiting double-degenerate binary, led to a more accurate analysis of its brightness variations. This 2009-2017 photometric study of DDO 44455 revealed a significant decline of 0.0003 +/- 0.0001 magnitude per year in its 40.5-minute orbital period. This photometric analysis confirmed that the binary's 40.5-minute eclipsing period is the most suitable for asteroseismology and nucleosynthesis calculations. Our brightness curve analysis suggests that our system is well-approximated by DNNE models, with a negligible third body influence. Moreover, our 2018-2019 photometric study showed a notable 0.012 +/- 0.002 magnitude outburst in April 2019, which is likely due to an outburst in this cataclysmic variable system.

This study proposes a novel approach to aggregating data from multiple populations, utilizing optimal transport plans to create a global summary. We examine various applications of this method in creating a global representation of customer behavior and its impact on business strategy. To address practical challenges, such as the presence of empty bins and discrete data, which complicate traditional transport problems, we use $p$-Wasserstein distances and introduce an ideal transport scheme. This scheme allows for the simultaneous aggregation of data and calculation of individual-wise distances to the global representation. By providing theoretical and empirical support for this method, we show that it offers multiple benefits for global data analysis.

The types of active galactic nuclei (AGN) classified as radio-loud or type II/III have distinct characteristics in terms of their host galaxies and large-scale structure alignments. Our study, utilizing the SDSS dataset, aimed to identify any correlations between the host galaxies of these AGN types and their surrounding cosmic structures. Type II AGN tend to reside in older and more metal-rich environments than their type I counterparts, while type radii sources exhibit similar properties to type I AGN. However, type radii sources exhibit weaker anisotropic excess than their type I counterparts. Furthermore, type radii sources and type I AGN display different alignment properties with respect to cosmic fiber structures. While type I AGN show increased alignment as redshift increases, type radii sources and type II AGN do not. Additionally, type radii sources and type II AGN are more aligned than their type I counterparts. Our findings also indicate that type radii sources and type II AGN are more likely to reside in void regions and underdense areas, but their intrinsic alignment properties do not affect this distribution.

This paper investigates complete flat rotation surfaces with pointwise 1-type Gaussian maps in the Euclidean space E^4, with a focus on diagonal matrices. It is established that a rotation surface with a given matrix type is of pointwise 1-type if and only if it consists of a flat plane in E^4.

A significant breakthrough in semantic segmentation has been achieved through the
advancement of self-supervised depth assessment techniques in monocular settings.
These techniques, which do not rely on annotated data, offer significant
advantages in terms of both time and resources. Numerous approaches, however,
have found success by leveraging pre-trained image classification models. More
recently, it has been demonstrated that self-supervised depth assessment
techniques can yield even better results than these classifications in downstream
segmentation tasks. In an effort to validate this discovery, we conduct a
comprehensive comparison of image classification and monocular depth
assessment pre-training techniques on downstream segmentation tasks. Through our
experiments, we successfully demonstrate that monocular depth assessment does
indeed offer substantial benefits in terms of downstream segmentation
performance, with an average improvement of 4.5% in the mean intersection over
union (mIoU) over several datasets. As such, we encourage the adoption of these
techniques in downstream segmentation applications and provide the pre-trained
models that we have generated for downstream evaluation purposes.

Current high-performance text-based Timeline Model learning methods are heavily reliant on specific domains and require substantial manual input for causal structure definition, making them impractical for use across various domains. In contrast, our novel framework, TCube, can generate domain-applicable time-series storytelling without the need for manual intervention by directly learning from raw time-series data and natural language descriptions. TCube's approach is based on integrating sequential event generation with temporal structure learning, effectively bypassing the need for manual timeline model definitions. TCube achieves this by jointly learning to generate sequential event descriptions that align with the intrinsic temporal structure of time-series data, drawn from its inherent geometric characteristics. TCube outperforms existing state-of-the-art topic model and neural timeline model learning methods, while also demonstrating superior performance to fully supervised neural timeline model learning approaches in a diverse, real-world benchmark dataset from a specific domain.

The ATLAS experiment at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) has conducted in-depth studies on the area of beauty meson physics, focusing particularly on $B_{s,d}$ meson transitions and some $D$-meson physics investigations. Relevant findings are presented here with evaluations of the associated systematic and statistical uncertainties. Additionally, development plans for enhanced analysis capabilities within future LHC datasets are discussed.

On a Cayley tree, we analyze the Ising model and examine its weak periodic configurations when the interaction matrix follows a specific pattern. For the case of a bipartite graph, we prove the existence of unique local configurations and periodic configurations with a cycle of two, given certain inequalities involving the interaction matrix elements. However, on a non-bipartite Cayley tree, no weakly periodic configurations with a cycle of two exist.

A new type of hyperbolic Cauchy problem with logarithmically varying coefficients has been defined, and it is characterized by its coefficients changing by a power of $p \ge 1$ and its principal part, along with all lower-order terms, being not more than $O\left( \frac{1}{p \ln p} \right)$ as $p$ increases. A proof has been provided that this problem is well-posed for any $p > e$.

The process of term segmentation, specifically for Japanese languages, has been extensively researched. Traditionally, this task was approached using supervised methods that heavily relied on extensive term alignment data and sophisticated models, such as hidden Markov models and neural networks. These methods, however, often demanded the creation of manually aligned term data, which was extremely laborious to generate. In this paper, we introduce the JSTEM model, an innovative Japanese term segmentation method based on the short-term memory of neural networks. By leveraging a vast amount of web crawlers that require accurate Japanese term segmentation, JSTEM can effectively improve its performance through self-supervised pre-training. Following joint fine-tuning with standard NLP tasks, the efficacy of the pre-trained JSTEM was evaluated, revealing superior accuracy compared to established competitive baselines. In particular, the accuracy of JSTEM surpassed 94% in accurately segmenting commonly occurring terms, specifically those terms that appeared frequently in both training and testing datasets.

Programmers frequently seek additional information beyond what they find on platforms like Stack Overflow. This research examines external links shared on Stack Overflow, with a focus on how developers utilize and benefit from these connections. The study found that the most shared links originate from prominent platforms like GitHub and Twitter. The findings also indicate that developers view these external connections as a bridge between the Stack Overflow community and the broader one, and that the shared links are often perceived as valuable for recognizing high-quality contributors outside of the platform. The results of this research are valuable for developers, organizations, and Stack Overflow administrators, and may provide a foundation for further studies on the shared external links on community-driven platforms.

By analyzing new findings from galaxy spectroscopy, it's evident that the properties of galaxies cannot be described by two parameters, rather there are at least six interlinked characteristics that need to be considered. There are at least two potential issues that need to be addressed, one being the missing galaxy problem, the severity of which is now more apparent. In this research, four potential solutions to the missing galaxy problem are critically examined, each of which, when individually evaluated, fails to fully account for the quantity of galaxies found in each phase of the galaxy lifecycle. However, there are other, more subtle signs of a missing galaxy issue, which we explore in relation to two particular aspects of galaxy evolution, namely the distribution of galaxy sizes and galaxy interaction patterns. Both of these signs are severely affected by the newly acquired knowledge, resulting in large discrepancies between predicted and actual galaxy counts.

Effective climate communication is essential to empower individuals to take action against the climate crisis, yet essential climate data is often scattered or overly technical, making it difficult to create effective educational materials about the climate. Although various climate data repositories exist, they present climate data in technical formats that require expertise to utilize, making it difficult for climate communicators to create informative and engaging content. To address this issue, we developed a Climate Information Repository specifically designed to facilitate easier access to climate data for climate communicators, reflecting a commitment to climate justice by putting vital climate data within reach of those who need it to effect change. As part of this commitment, we also established a Community Advisory Board to ensure that the repository serves the communities it aims to support through collaborative development and provide direct climate data to those who require it to initiate effect change. This two-pronged approach to promoting climate justice through technological development showcases the potential of technology to effect positive change within the climate movement through the Climate Information Repository and Climate Data Portal. This project is funded by the PII's Equity, Diversity, and Inclusion Committee.

Domain Generalization (DG) plays a crucial role in real-world NLP applications operating in high-risk domains such as medicine. Developing a robust DG model for event extraction in medical notes proves particularly challenging due to several factors, including domain discrepancy, label noise, and semantic ambiguity inherent in medical semantics. This study tackles these obstacles by introducing a novel framework, GO-DG (Generalization through Obscuring for Domain Generalization), which intentionally obfuscates source domain data to create a network of relationships among various domains, thereby enhancing the model's ability to generalize across different domains. Furthermore, a theoretical analysis is provided to validate its efficacy. To evaluate its performance, a new sign event extraction dataset specific to medical notes is created and a model pre-trained on this dataset is integrated into the proposed framework. Experimental results outperform existing state-of-the-art domain generalization methods in sign event extraction task by a significant 2.12% in exact match F1 score.

Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) has emerged as a promising solution to the complex self-driving problem, outperforming traditional control theories in many ways. However, DRL still faces several obstacles in self-driving applications, particularly in establishing a clear reward structure, navigating dynamic and diverse environments, and ensuring the safety of learning processes. To address these challenges, we have developed an advanced DL-based system that leverages a novel, context-sensitive reward function, an simulated driving environment with randomized elements, and a transfer learning strategy that prioritizes safety, to systematically explore and improve driving policies in the virtual environment before deploying the optimized model in real vehicles.

Categorizing data into distinct groups is a fundamental task in machine learning. Traditionally, this problem has been approached using methods rooted in linear algebra, such as support vector machines and nearest neighbor classifiers. More recently, attention has turned to using attention-based transformers for classification tasks. In our research, we introduce a novel, spiking neural network approach that leverages the power of efficient computation to perform categorization tasks near real-time. We build upon previous work in categorization problems by integrating the advantages of efficient spiking computation and a highly adaptable random neural network architecture. This innovative design utilizes random networks to achieve universal approximation capabilities, while employng spiking neurons to enable efficient computation and near real-time prediction capabilities. We use learning to map input data to a codebook, enabling efficient computation on spiking neurons and accurate group identification. Further enhancements to our algorithm enable learning without teacher feedback, as well as rapid retraining with minimal teacher input to keep the model current. We validate our research by comparing group definitions across various domains, including text, image, and signed values.

The thermal stability of Strange Quark Stars at high temperatures in the presence of strong magnetic fields is investigated, with particular focus on their spin alignment properties. By examining the alignment of quarks within the star, we derive a modified equation of state, which is then used to plot $T-c_{s}^{2}$ diagrams for both thermal and zero-temperature conditions, allowing for a direct comparison and assessment of the impact of temperature on these stars. Additionally, we plot the impact of magnetic field strength on these diagrams, with $T-c_{s}^{2}$ diagrams at finite temperatures and strong magnetic fields showing a spin-aligned phase that is absent under zero-field conditions. This aligned phase is found to significantly impact the star's metric properties, with strong fields causing an inner and outer radius contraction, as well as an increase in mass. This contraction is found to be more pronounced at strong fields than at zero-field, with a maximal effect seen at a strong field of $10^{33}$ Gauss, with the star's mass, radius, and entropy all demonstrating sensitivity to both temperature and strong magnetic field effects.

Scientific research has greatly benefited from high-performance computing systems.
However, the resources provided by such systems are typically only available to
a select group of researchers due to their significant costs and limited capacity.
To bridge this gap, we developed Pando, a system that allows anyone to join a
research project by becoming an individual volunteer on a standard laptop or
desktop computer. Each Pando node runs as a separate process within its host
operating system and features a comprehensive set of libraries for running code
in various languages, thus providing ample resources for a diverse range of users.
Security is ensured through the use of signed certificates, protecting Pando
nodes from unauthorized access. By gathering and sharing the computational
capacity of individual volunteer nodes, Pando offers a more inclusive and
equitable platform to which every researcher can contribute, thereby enhancing
collaboration and expanding access to high-performance computing resources.

The computational discovery of eigenissues associated with complex, large-scale nonlinear eigenproblems is a crucial aspect in numerous engineering and scientific applications. Various strategies have been proposed to resolve these eigenproblems by transforming them into affine eigenproblems, which can subsequently be solved using the robust Ritz value-based method, originally designed for bounded domains in spectral approximation of operator issues. However, the nonstationary or time-varying nature of some eigenproblems limits the applicability of these approaches. In this context, we present a novel variant of the Ritz value-based method, minimal rational interpolation, which is better suited for the estimation of nonlinear, time-varying eigenissues. Our theoretical analysis confirms that the proposed method is robust and an initial set of trial vectors can be used to accurately compute eigenissues in successive time-steps. Moreover, the method requires significantly fewer trial vectors when eigenissues remain consistent across consecutive time-steps. Numerical tests demonstrate the method's efficacy and robustness.

Investigating the connections between different bases is an important area of study in number theory. Specifically, we are focusing on the concept of "intermediate $\beta$-transformation," which is a greedy approach to transferring numbers from a weaker base $\beta$ with limited arithmetic operations to a stronger base $G$ with full arithmetic operations. By applying this transformation to the special base $(1+\sqrt{D})/2$, we show that the resulting number can be expressed as a combination of powers of $D$ and $\sqrt{D}$ with coefficients restricted to $\{-1,0,1\}$.

This phenomenon is further confirmed by the nonvanishing of a certain combination of vector and axial-vector currents, which is consistent with the partial restoration of a subgroup of $SU(2)_{L}\times SU(2)_{R}$ (for $N_{c}=3$) or $SO(N_{f})$ (for $N_{c}\geq 3$) within the vacuum. Machine learning models, such as random forests and decision trees, are popular choices in various fields due to their high predictive accuracy and ability to handle complex data. However, their 'black box' nature makes it difficult to understand how they reach a prediction, which is a significant drawback when analyzing data like medical records. This paper introduces an approach called disentangled assignment curves (DACs) to visualize the inner workings of these models and identify key features that influence their predictions. By extending previous research on feature importance, DACs offer a visual representation of a model's feature effects, allowing users to inspect global and local model behavior. We evaluate the effectiveness of DACs using synthetic data and a real-world medical dataset, showcasing their potential in interpreting predictions made by these models.

Inclining towards personalized machine learning models and protecting sensitive data has sparked an interest, leading to significant advancements and innovations. Deep learning models and their underlying data often attract high value and potential security risks due to data leakage during the training process. To address these challenges, a novel framework called Flatee is introduced to facilitate the collaborative training of machine learning models within and across isolated, secure environments provided by various hardware-based security solutions. Flatee framework innovatively combines the federated learning and differential privacy approaches to support collaborative training across isolated security domains and achieves secure communication through encryption and secret sharing protocols. A comprehensive analysis of Flatee's theoretical constraints is provided, evaluating the associated privacy loss and model accuracy loss in the process. To validate Flatee's functionality and performance, empirical evaluations are conducted across three real-world datasets, demonstrating its efficiency and accuracy in enabling confidential collaborative training.

The increased use of compact integrated systems in the aerospace and defense sectors has led to a need for advanced operator monitoring and evaluation methods. Research has shown that assessing an operator's performance in these systems is crucial for optimizing efficiency, ensuring safety, and boosting overall productivity. Evaluating an operator's footprint, a concept representing their impact on the system, is a complex task due to the high-dimensional and non-linear nature of the data involved. To address this challenge, our study develops an automated approach for calculating operator footprint in multi-dimensional spaces using machine learning and data analysis. Our proposed approach employs a novel data representation technique, known as operator fingerprinting, to convert complex operator behavior data into a compact and easily interpretable format. Using this fingerprint, we calculate the footprint using a variety of machine learning algorithms and feature selection methods. Our proposed approach outperforms existing operator assessment methods in terms of accuracy and computational efficiency, as demonstrated by our comprehensive simulation studies and real-world applications. Our automated operator footprint calculation method offers a valuable and versatile tool for operator performance analysis and contributes to the development of more effective and efficient integrated systems.

Constrained enterprise applications pose significant difficulties in reverse engineering, particularly when attempting to reverse engineer containerized applications, which is a crucial process for creating container security policies. Volatile and diverse system call behaviors make learning system call rules for reverse engineering containerized applications an intractable task. Our solution, Timeloops, is a static system call rule learning engine specifically designed for reverse engineering containerized applications. It uses a containerized Dynamic Linking Component (DLC) to analyze system call behavior over time and employs a custom search algorithm to learn system call rules, which can be improved using a feedback mechanism through interplay with a dynamic analysis component, which is helpful for reverse engineering challenges. Our extensive experiments on real containerized applications reveal that Timeloops can automatically learn accurate system call rules, which are more precise and flexible than existing system call rule sets. Furthermore, we demonstrate that Timeloops can successfully solve a wide range of practical containerized application security problems, including an authentic containerized application ransomware reverse engineering case study.

Recent advancements in NLP item-based representations, such as word and word piece embeddings, have greatly enhanced the performance of various tasks including recommendation systems and online classifiers. By utilizing their geometric properties, we successfully developed a classifier that outperformed traditional methods like SVM and logistic regression on recommendation tasks using sparse user-item matrices. Our linear classifier in the shape of an hyperplane constructed from user and item embeddings offered notable performance gains without the need for increased model complexity.

This study provides a reliable method to track the distribution of different stellar populations near a massive black hole, accounting for the movement of individual stars and their different energy levels. Using simulations that model various initial distributions of stars from different energy levels, the research shows that a self-organized distribution of these stars is achieved within a few hundred thousand years to a few million years. This outcome aligns with the theoretically predicted distribution formula by Hills (1988), which is not affected by the specific way the stars were initially spread out, a previously untested assumption. Furthermore, this study finds that a more accurate understanding of the distribution can be obtained when modeling the movement of individual stars rather than relying on continuous fluid models. Although both a previously proposed formula by Merrifield (1996) and a different distribution by Volonteri et al. (2007) fail to accurately describe the actual distribution of all stars, they both correctly predict the distribution of high energy level stars independently of their low energy counterparts. Additionally, this study discovers that a particular type of star with very low energy level moves in the opposite direction of the massive black hole's movement, an effect that can be calculated using a simple adjustment to the theoretical distribution formula by Hills (1988). These findings are then used to analyze the distribution of different stellar populations in the nuclear star cluster of a nearby galaxy, using a range of theoretical and observational constraints to refine our understanding of the cluster's formation and evolution.

This regulation simulation explores the efficacy of utilizing Model Predictive Control (MPC) as an efficient method for resource allocation in diverse scenarios. The proposed solution employs (R)MPC, a method that optimizes an instance-specific cost function while predicting and optimizing system dynamics over a limited horizon. (R)MPC is reoptimized at each iteration based on instances of randomness or periodic changes. The simulation assesses (R)MPC's performance under both random and periodically evolving scenarios.

This paper offers a theoretical framework for linear dimensionality reduction,
a problem where the input data is modeled as a product of two unknown matrices,
one low-dimensional and sparse, under a compressive sampling process. It is
demonstrated in this study that when the matrices satisfy certain conditions,
it is possible to achieve a near-optimal reconstruction using a single iteration
of a simplified version of the conjugate gradient method with an especially simple
and effective random preconditioner, reducing the computational complexity from
O(n^2) to O(nlog^2(n)). Additionally, the paper introduces a novel technique for
estimating the influence of noise during the optimization process, which is used
to develop a simple algorithm for regularized recovery and is shown to be robust
even in the presence of noise levels exceeding 100%. This algorithm is further
equipped with techniques for handling data corruption using an outlying column
rejection method, resulting in improved performance on synthetic data and eBay
data as well as with the ability to accurately reconstruct images corrupted by
random noise or adversarial attacks.

The system has two types of agents with opposing colonization methods: global colonization for empty site occupation and local colonization requiring empty neighboring sites.  One agent represents an aggressive species that outcompetes others, while the other two are competitors with the second attempting to coexist.  Numerical studies on systems mimicking plant canopy dynamics reveal that when there are few chisels, only the aggressive species can compete effectively.  However, intermediate levels of chaos allow coexistence, indicating that intermediate disorder can benefit species competition.  Nevertheless, frequent aerial colonization can lead to the exclusion of the more nuanced competitor.

This study develops a formalism in abelian quantum dual field theory to define a type of von Neumann algebras with spatial finiteness and demonstrates their equivalence to those in abelian quantum fluid dynamics. The research also establishes the existence and uniqueness of von Neumann algebras within specific nets of spatially-defined double cones. The relations between these formalisms are examined through rigorous mathematical proof. Furthermore, it is proven that there is a natural equivalence between the categories of these two sets of algebras, thereby showing their intrinsic connection.

Our study demonstrates how to generate and improve magnon-photon-phonor entanglement, a complex phenomenon that arises in a spin-wave based magnomechanical system with interconnected light and sound waves. This entanglement can be detected and quantified using a specific criterion that measures the degree of continuous variable entanglement. As primary components, we assume the involvement of an optical cavity, a magnetic material, and an oscillator. Notably, we demonstrate that incorporating a feedback circuit, where the output photons from a microwave resonator interact with either the magnon or the phonon, significantly enhances magnon-photon-phonor entanglement. Furthermore, our findings are supported by a numerical example, which also explores the impact of dissipation and the initial state on entanglement dynamics, yielding a condition necessary for its generation.

Within the dimensionally-regulated QCD framework, our dimensionally-recursively developed set of triple-collinear splitting operators in a specific basis lacks explicit expression due to its basis-dependent nature and a non-invertible transformation matrix. However, our recently established recursive relationship for these operators allows us to efficiently compute higher-order members of this basis, thereby accelerating our all-order decomposition of one-loop triple-collinear singularities in terms of these operators.

A formal proof for the Neron Desingularization, a multidimensional variant of Hensel's Lemma, has been provided, which generalizes prior constructive proofs and relates to key algorithms in algebraic number theory and $p$-adic computation. For a specific type of one-dimensional local ring, a constructive version of Neron Desingularization is formulated, which can be viewed as a complex extension of a finite number of simple resolutions. This version generalizes finite simple resolutions and relates to the algorithm used to construct Kuranishi families of singularities. The construction involves the use of Grobner basis and Hilbert's 16th problem for resolving singularities of a specific type of surface, which is a constant sequence of transformations that in each step involves the blowup of a specific ideal and solving differential equations to obtain normalized forms of power series and find normalized forms of power series that satisfy certain valuation conditions. The construction of Grobner basis and Hilbert's 16th problem for resolving singularities of a specific type of surface, which is a constant sequence of transformations that in each step involves the blowup of a specific ideal and solving differential equations to obtain normalized forms of power series that satisfy certain valuation conditions.

The Indonesian archipelago's sundials are scattered landmarks that serve as historical, cultural, and scientific icons, yet their physical preservation is challenged by their exposed outdoor settings, leading to wear and tear. In an effort to address this, the Suryakala NusantarA project (SKA) aims to document the existing sundials in Indonesia by creating a comprehensive digital archive. Each sundial is meticulously mapped, mapped, and recorded in 3D, enabling the project to monitor their condition over time. By analyzing the geometry of each sundial, the project also calculates the local gnomon angle and latitude to further document their unique features.

This correspondence explores a novel integrated data and power transfer (IDPN)
solved component approach to dual function D2D comms assisted by a IRS system,
where the IRS helps optimize both the DC and AC powered D2D link success rates.
Firstly, it's noted that the IRS can be modeled as a set of complex coefficients.
These are then broken down into two parts: a part that's optimized through
convexification and another that's modeled as a circuit and managed through
optimal power allocation. Secondly, a multi-dimensional weighted MM method is
used to convexify the non-convex problem, while an optimal power allocation
approach is also developed to maximize the product of DC and AC powered D2D
success rates under power constraints. Thirdly, a joint power allocation and
IRS optimization technique is implemented through an iterative process, leading
to the final solution. Through numerical experiments, the effectiveness of the
proposed solution is also demonstrated in terms of its performance benefits.

To obtain detailed flow information in complex environments, particularly around the aircraft fuselage, researchers are exploring the use of Laser Doppler Anemometry (LDA) as a remote, contactless measurement technique. Our team investigated the feasibility of employing a single LDA beam to make 2D velocity measurements in three dimensions by utilizing a specialized tripod setup and advanced imaging software to automatically locate and control the LDA beam's position via a robotic system. This approach involved scanning the LDA beam across a test section in a step-by-step manner to collect 3D velocity data at predefined points. Our results demonstrate the viability of this technique for remote 2D and 3D velocity measurements in complex geometries, offering a novel approach to flow analysis in the aerospace industry and other applications requiring precise velocity measurements in complex environments.

This note begins by defining the concept of a first-order spectrum with binary links and then explores its characteristics using a graphical approach to illustrate the underlying binary relationships.

The development of phase disks has greatly improved the imaging capabilities of transmission electron microscopes (TEM), allowing researchers to detect fine details in various materials. However, the limited range of operations performed by current phase disks may lead to image distortions in samples that have already been optimized for conventional TEM imaging. We propose the use of programmable phase disks to dynamically adjust phase and amplitude during imaging to improve fine details in samples. A programmable phase disk based on a hybrid superconducting-coil liquid-ammonia magnet can effectively replace or supplement fixed-phase objects to perform focused ion beam (FIB) and transmission electron microscopy (TEM) without leading to sample degradation. We demonstrate the potential of our prototype by successfully imaging fine features of a lithium niobate crystal, including its domain walls, without compromising its integrity for further analysis.

A function is proposed to calculate polynomial assessment at non-uniformly
spaced points while preserving a specified number of zero values and fulfilling
a linear difference inequality of a specified order with respect to a given
norm. As an application of this function, an optimally weighted geometric
inequality of the G. G. Mastrovescu type is derived for the second difference of
functions that are zero at the vertices of a square.
