This work focuses on double-faced auctions that have been verified as reliable, where a throughput function through(x) is used to determine a throughput action. A corresponding price p(x) is also set using a pricing function. In double-faced auctions with a limited number of participants, it has been established that there are previously unknown, yet reliable methods for implementing functions that ensure reliability, where both the bid and ask prices are established as a result of a mechanism's outcome. These mechanisms are efficient and efficient there exist scenarios in which their efficiency is known to be limited to a factor of 3, and this limitation appears to be unavoidable. Additionally, there are reliable methods that are efficient and efficient it can be proven that any double-faced auction that is reliable must involve at least two rounds of exchanges. These methods have been known to be reliable even when the number of participants is not known in advance, and in such cases, there are known methods that are both efficient and efficient any double-faced auction that is reliable must involve a minimum of a certain number of rounds of exchanges.

Our analysis of HQET and its applications to the examination of FLAVOR changing neutral currents in heavy quark systems has led to a significant understanding heavy quark symmetry constraints on the amplitude and ratio of certain key matrix elements. These key matrix elements are crucial in the calculation of direct CP violation in the decay of certain mesons, particularly D-mesons. Analysis of direct CP violation in the decays of D-mesons, particularly D-s mesons, can provide valuable insights into the mechanisms underlying these phenomena. Research on direct CP violation in the decays of D-s mesons, particularly in the examination of FLAVOR changing neutral currents, has therefore become a crucial area of study.

The study of the decomposition of a given mapping into an asymmetric monotonically non-decreasing function and a symmetric component, as well as their periodic counterparts, is explored in this research. Consequently, the characteristics of a nonexpansive curve are described.

A popular technique, known as Dynamic Mode Decomposition, has various applications in analyzing complex systems with nonlinear characteristics and extensive data sets, despite its effectiveness, it poses challenges in practical implementation due to memory limitations and complex matrix operations, a new approach using kernel methods has been introduced to tackle these limitations and improve its feasibility, a specific kernel kernel Education for LANDO) method has been developed for efficient optimization in resource-constrained environments and extensive datasets, it includes an efficient kernel matrix construction strategy to minimize storage requirements, a data reduction technique using kernel-based marginal relevance maximization to focus on the most relevant data, it enables the use of sparse solvers for rapid computation and thus its feasibility in real-time applications, a detailed analysis and numerical experiments demonstrate its performance and robustness and it is now publicly available for use.

This study examines the patterns of decisions made by Goethe's characters in a specific scene from Faust, analyzing the intricacy and similarity of their choices. By measuring the information content of their decisions, we gain insight into the intricacy of their decision-making process, while comparing their choices to the full range of available options reveals the level of constraint they face. Additionally, their similarities are assessed to determine their resemblance to one another. These calculations are calculated in relation to the entire set of available lines from The Faerie Queene, providing a broader context for our analysis. Our findings are derived from the text of The Faerie Queene, and are supplemented by additional calculations involving chess openings, which have become increasingly relevant due to the strategic importance of early game decisions in competitive play.

We've developed a novel approach using pale dwarf stars to precisely determine millisecond pulsar (MSP) parameters in a binary system. By analyzing pale dwarf parameters and incorporating them with MSP orbital data, we can significantly enhance our knowledge of MSP characteristics, especially in cases where data is scarce. Our method leverages information from pale dwarf stars, which are extremely low-luminosity objects, to derive MSP parameters with greater accuracy. We've applied this method to a dataset of 43 pulsars and derived their parameters, which we then used to recalculate their orbital periods and compare the results to existing data, especially in cases where data is scarce. Our analysis has also allowed us to derive the spin period of the star PSR J0030+0440's companion, which we found to be 3.22 days.

A comprehensive study on motion descriptors for Lagrangian dynamics of an arbitrary order in an n-dimensional space is presented, specifically focusing on order 1 for both homogeneous and non-homogeneous cases. Key concepts such as nonlocal variables, motions, homogenizations, and complete reductions are rigorously defined within this framework. The analysis relies heavily on the use of higher-order Lagrangian fields, higher-order connections, and complete differential operators, all of which are heavily based on modern geometric theories of differential equations. The resulting methods and concepts can be extensively applied to a wide range of mechanical systems, including higher-order Lagrangian systems, constraints, and multibody systems with constraints. The presented methods are particularly relevant and useful in the fields of theoretical and applied mechanics.

This paper introduces a method for creating and retrieving complex 3D objects through a virtual reality environment where users can draw in air to form a desired object's shape. In this shape-based retrieval approach, users can also modify an existing object's shape by modifying some of its features to create a new one. Our research focuses on developing a system for air-drawing in 3D VR and another for retrieving shapes by altering specific parts of a 3D model. We utilize the Mediatek MT7622 processor and the motion capture device Optitrack to register and capture spatial data in a real 3D space and a two-dimensional plane. We translate user-drawn lines into smooth curves and also smooth out polygonal edges of existing shapes to match the user's intent more accurately. We're developing a system that allows for the creation of complex, custom 3D shapes through air-drawing in a 3D space and for modifying features on existing shapes to create new ones.

HD80606b, a planet with a 112-day orbit around its host star, experiences a highly eccentric orbit that causes its periastron passage to last only 2.5 hours under intense radiation. Understanding of its orbital timing has been hindered due to insufficient periastron timing measurements taken close to the periastron and only a few scattered observations throughout its entire orbit. However, a 12-month study of HD80606b, conducted using the transit method, utilized a global network of seven telescopes and retrieved 101 transit spectra to accurately measure its periastron passage times. By incorporating additional parameters, this timing data allows for a comprehensive revision of its orbital parameters, resulting in a highly precise periastron timing measurement with a standard deviation of 5.5 seconds. Furthermore, its predicted periastron passage times for 2023-2026 are determined to guarantee that the James Webb Space Telescope can effectively capture its entire thermal emission spectrum during its periastron passage.

Research into gravitational wave detection in the high-frequency range has led to the examination of compact astrophysical objects that undergo collapse into singularities. For isentropic collapse with a pressure parameter of the form $p = kp$, where $0 \le k < 1/3$, it has been established that the feasibility of such an isentropic collapse depends on the value of $k$. Specifically, if $k > 0$, both the density and pressure decrease as the singularity is approached, resulting in an unbounded pressure only at the singularity itself. Conversely, if $k = 0$, an isentropic collapse results in density increasing while pressure remains constant, causing pressure to decouple from gravity at late times and preventing collapse. If $k < 0$, both density and pressure increase as the singularity is approached, but pressure can exceed gravitational force, potentially preventing collapse. We have determined that for a state equation of the form $p = k\rho c^2$, where $0 \le \rho < \rho_0 < \infty$ and $0 \le k < 1/3$, both density and pressure must decrease in order to allow collapse, implying that density cannot exceed its initial value, contradicting assumed conditions. This result holds for all values of $k$, even when $k < 0$, where density and pressure both increase, but pressure can become the dominant force, potentially preventing collapse.

Hacking and Unruh originally suggested a method of deriving the first law of black hole thermodynamics using Iyer-Wald's approach, which they did by framing it within a framework of generalized diffeomorphism, leading to a combination of horizon area, temperature, and entropy being inversely proportional to the square of a constant, $\Gamma$. This paper generalizes Unruh-Hawking's original idea to black holes in more complex spacetimes and a wider range of thermodynamic parameters, which are determined through the use of Killing vectors in extremal black holes, which have specific properties that simplify this framework, which ultimately leads to a new expression for the entropy of an extremal black hole in terms of its mass and angular momentum being inversely proportional to the square of a constant, \Gamma, which provides a fresh perspective on the thermodynamics of these complex black holes, which ultimately leads to a new expression for the entropy of an extremal black hole in terms of its mass and angular momentum being inversely proportional to the square of a constant, \Gamma, which provides a fresh perspective on the thermodynamics of these complex black holes, which ultimately leads to a new expression for the entropy of an extremal black hole in terms of its mass and angular momentum being inversely proportional to the square of a constant, \Gamma, which provides a fresh perspective on the thermodynamics of these complex black holes.

To effectively utilize engine expertise, it's crucial to utilize engine knowledge for training foundation models, but the varying lengths of engine experience data pose significant challenges for effective training. These challenges include unpredictable gradients and an imbalance in training data samples across different engine learning stages, which can hinder the model's performance. In order to overcome these obstacles, we propose two novel methods: 1) employing variable learning rate control to fine-tune the model's learning speed based on the influence of each data sample, and 2) artificially expanding shorter experience data samples by pairing them with data samples from later stages of engine learning. Experimental results on diverse datasets demonstrate that our methods significantly outperform existing approaches and yield state-of-the-art performance, achieving new records on two benchmark datasets while user-friendly implementation codes are available at the provided URL.

A dynamic approach to the quantized, flexible Poincaré algebra is developed within a path integral framework. Its core concept lies in treating the parameters of the internal symmetry, such as momentum and angular momentum, as Poincaré transformation parameters. Poincaré invariant path integrands are constructed using the parameters' cons equations, allowing for the derivation of an effective action for a field theory with a diffeomorphism invariant path integral measure. At the one-loop level, a non-abelian particle action is found, with the internal group being $SO(1,3)$. Utilizing the se(1,3) symmetry, a graviton action is derived, with the same non-abelian form and dependence on $k^2 R^2$. Both the graviton and particle actions are found not to be non-minimally coupled to the curvature, although the non-abelian nature of the coupling suggests an indirect influence. We use the principle of least action to demonstrate that the obtained particle and graviton actions are not the only possible non-abelian actions invariant under diffeomorphisms and Lorentz transformations, with the principle of least action playing a pivotal role in eliminating non-minimally coupled terms.

This research introduces algorithmic techniques for highlighting specific sub-problems in the issue of upward planarity testing and reconstruction. Utilizing parameterized sub-problem approaches, the authors develop a linear-time reconstruction algorithm for upward planarity. Furthermore, the findings extend to a new understanding of horizontal 1-bend right-monotone drawing, achieving an $f(n,\beta)$ time complexity, where n represents the number of vertices in a directed graph, and $\beta$ its face count.

Effectively navigating through a previously visited location using memory is the core of human spatial navigation.  This skill  is  being  applied  broadly  in  robotics  and  computer  vision  today.  However,  previous  approaches  to  memory-based  navigation  reattached  every  possible  past  experience,  resulting  in  too  many  memory  fragments  being  used  as  guidance.  This  problem  is  a  manifestation  of  the  well-known  "better-than-necessary"  issue  in  machine  learning,  limiting  the  efficiency  of  these  applications.  To  overcome  this  problem,  we  have  developed  the  MemoNav  system,  which  selectively  filters  out  irrelevant  past  experiences  when  navigating.  This  innovative  system  consists  of  two  key  modules:  the  first  filters  out  uninformative  memory  fragments,  while  the  second  evaluates  the  value  of  each  remaining  fragment  to  direct  the  navigation.  Experimental  results  show  that  using  memo navigation  saves  up  to  80%  of  computational  resources  while  reducing  navigation  navigation  navigation  navigation  navigation  navigation  navigation  navigation  navigation  navigation  navigation  navigation

The advent of the 4G era brought about a fundamental shift in wireless network architecture with the introduction of the eNodeB. Before 4G, Base Transceiver Stations dominated the landscape, but 4G's requirements for high data rates, low latency, and enhanced link capacity gave rise to the compact eNodeB. This compact infrastructure enabled a vast network of small cells to take root. In this article, the historical development of the compact eNodeB, its adoption within the 4G to 5G frameworks, and the prospects for its role in 6G are examined. Furthermore, the advantages and challenges associated with compact cells, along with current best practices for their deployment,DeenDeen future trends, are addressed.

In recent years, hypergraph frameworks have been proposed to explore the interplay between special structures and algorithms that are robust to algorithmic errors and noise. This paper generalizes this concept to more complex environments by extending it to hypergraphs with dynamic elements. We begin by generalizing the standard hypergraph framework to accommodate changes over time in the graph's components, and provide examples that illustrate the effectiveness of this broadened concept. Furthermore, we expand the analysis to include cases where the graph's vertices or edges may change, as well as scenarios where the graph itself is completely new. Lastly, we propose a theoretical model in which a change-detection algorithm must operate on a hypergraph with rare events embedded within normal patterns.

This review examines the equivalence and interconnections between key operator expansion techniques, specifically operator product expansion, Newton polygon operator expansion, and the more recent operator product pushforward expansion.

In an effort to gain a deeper understanding of the rate at which TMC decays, we carried out shell-model calculations and analyzed the medium effect's influence on the decay process. It was found that the medium effect significantly influences the decay process and cannot be disregarded in the analysis. As a result, we developed a new formalism for calculating the amplitude that accounts for the medium effect. It was found that, after taking the medium effect into account, it is possible to describe the direct-decay process even in environments that do not include the Hoyle state, using only two parameters.

A two-dimensional numerical investigation of dynamic fracture in elastic materials,
considering both flat and wavy crack paths, was conducted to identify the conditions under which oscillatory patterns emerge and tip branching occurs.
By utilizing a sharp interface hydrodynamic fracture model that incorporates both inherent time and length scales of materials,
the model successfully predicted the onset of oscillatory patterns and tip branching in elastic materials without considering their specific constitutive laws.
Moreover, the study found that the type of fracture pattern that forms at a given load level depends on the size of the material's inherent length scale,
with shorter length scales resulting in more localized damage and longer scales leading to more diffuse damage zones.

When transmitting compressed data over a channel with errors, knowing the original data helps the receiver use error correction codes effectively. Our study focuses on two questions: first, how does access to the source data at the encoder improve communication efficiency for finite data sets with feedback? And second, what are some simple methods the encoder can use to adapt its transmission to the actual data in use? Our research provides a mathematical framework to analyze this effect and also reveals that feedback's benefit is significantly reduced when the encoder can adjust its method of communication.

A unique class of superfluids known as topological superfluids exhibits flow without resistance and possesses non-trivial properties of topological nature. These are directly related to the creation of Fu-Kane Majorana zero modes, which have the potential to achieve logical operations within a unified system of topology and quantum mechanics, thus achieving 100% of the operation. Our research confirms through numerical computations that a specific type of model, an attractive version of the two-dimensional Rashba Hubbard model with less than half-filled band, can support both superfluidity and topological properties when it has a singlet of a specific spin configuration. These findings offer a new perspective on the occurrence of topological superfluids in 2D systems based on fermionic particles and are consistent with a theoretical model representing interacting Rashba fermions at low levels of density that can be described by an effective theoretical approach known as the Rashba $p$-wave (or $d$-wave) Lee-Sarma model. We also observed that systems with a higher level of density can achieve topological superfluidity at certain compositions within the same model.

This study focuses on developing table-aware models for verifying data within tables and undertaking related proof-related tasks. We now detail our approach and associated datasets to be used in the SemEval-2021 task focused on table data within scientific papers, specifically validated through Crowdsourcing.

A graph G is considered shortened if G's vertices can cover all its edges. We've established a understanding of shortened graphs by determining which subsets of vertices serve as shortened resolvers, and also identified the minimum number of vertices required to serve this purpose. Additionally, a condition was established for when a shortened graph has this minimum number of vertices, and some examples were provided along with an exploration of its implications in maps and networks.

The effectiveness of merging ultraviolet radiation at 313 nm and ozone for removing sulfur compounds in flue gas has been investigated in our study. This investigation is based on kinetic principles and uses real-time data from an experimental system that generates ozone via an ultraviolet lamp and subsequently transforms it into active oxygen in the presence of SO2 and SO3. The results reveal that adding an ozone generator significantly increases the efficiency of ultraviolet radiation for converting SO2 into SO3, particularly in low-heat flue gas containing 0.005% SO2. Specifically, when using an ozone generator producing 500000 oz (300) per hour and applying ultraviolet radiation with an area of 0.02 m2, the SO2 to SO3 conversion efficiency increased from 0.0000045% to 0.000025%. The study further indicates that utilizing an ozone generator without ultraviolet radiation is less efficient for processing low-heat flue gas, as it primarily converts SO2 into SO3 on cell walls rather than in the gas itself.

As neural and synaptic computation research gains momentum, simulating neuromorphic systems is becoming crucial. Using a system-on-a-chip approach, non-atomic operations can be modeled, studying the interplay between algorithms and hardware. However, current simulators fail to meet the needs of neuroscientists and computer engineers due to their limited flexibility and isolated implementation. In response, we have developed a comprehensive, modular, and concurrent simulation framework based on SystemC. It models various spike-time encoding methods and neural network hardware, allowing for the seamless integration of research findings into the simulation model. The framework's versatility is showcased through multiple simulation examples, while an open-source implementation is provided for the Memristor-Backed Binary Vector Encoding (BBVE) method and Schmitt-Trigger Leaky Integrate-and-Fire model, all accompanied by a user-friendly tutorial.

When evaluating the persuasiveness of text, the effectiveness of conventional machine learning and deep learning models is often hindered by the presence of ambiguous language. Many recent approaches have been developed to manage quantified expressions, but they are typically only able to process "all" and "none" and are usually embedded within controlled, closed-world environments. In contrast, our proposed "indecision forest" method draws inspiration from the decision-making of a rational individual who, when confronted with uncertain information, may choose not to make a definitive judgment. By extending decision trees to incorporate "indecision" as a possible outcome, our forest learning algorithm is able to process arguments that rely on probabilistic language such as "most" and "few." When applied to the task of assessing whether a paragraph supports, refutes, or fails to decisively support a subsequent sentence, our indecision forest model, when trained on the Amazon Reviews dataset, demonstrates a capacity to accurately classify paragraphs with quantified expressions like "all," "few," "many," and so on.

This paper investigates the computational efficiency of Dynamic Time Warping in a non-trivial context, specifically when dealing with large datasets and queries of long duration, leading to expensive calculations. We introduce a novel discarding principle based on CDW, designed to quickly eliminate time series that appear similar but have different timelines, a common challenge in AP-based methods. We demonstrate how to apply discarding not only in the early stages but also during the approximate nearest neighbor search process, significantly reducing Dynamic Time Warping computations by up to 94% with 9.4 times speedup with negligible loss in accuracy on real-world datasets.

This study investigates the effectiveness of inquiry-based test design feedback on university students' learning outcomes. The research focused on the causal link between such feedback and students' conceptual understanding, with a view to address the high cost and low success rates associated with defects found during software testing. To address a knowledge gap in the educational feedback literature, our study filled by analyzing how detailed feedback and inquiry-based feedback impact students' learning. The study involved an experimental design where detailed feedback and inquiry-based feedback were compared in a university software testing course. The results of our study show that inquiry-based feedback is a more effective teaching tool, as it leads to improved conceptual understanding and engages students in the learning process. The study found that students who received inquiry-based feedback had higher test scores and demonstrated higher levels of conceptual understanding as measured by the Conceptual Test Design Assessment. Furthermore, our study found that students who received inquiry-based feedback were more engaged in the learning process and demonstrated improved problem-solving skills. These findings suggest that inquiry-based feedback is a more effective teaching tool and can help to address the high cost and low success rates associated with software defects.

Recent studies have shown that Deep Neural Networks, although effective in numerous tasks, often lack transparency. Concept Analysis provides a framework for defining precise concepts through interactive inquiries. This study integrates Concept Analysis with Independent Learning of Rules, a prominent method in rule extraction from machine learning models, specifically targeting the clarification of deep neural networks. By combining the strengths of both approaches, we enable efficient and transparent explanation generation for INDOOR, a state-of-the-art indoor location classification system. Our approach facilitates the concept of 'left turn' within indoor navigation networks, allowing for a clear understanding of its indoor location context, along with a corresponding visual explanation.

Deep graph convolutional networks have significantly advanced graph representation learning, but they often produce low-quality node representations due to an excessive smoothing effect. This issue stems from convolutions that excessively average node information while aggregating local structural details. In an effort to address this limitation, we propose a novel, self-regulating graph convolutional network called the self-adjunct graph convolutional network, which effectively mitigates over-smoothing by taking into account both node and derivative information during feature learning. As a direct consequence of our self-adjunct design, we can accurately model high-order graph structure, thereby substantially enhancing node representation quality and data partitioning capability. Experimental results confirm the efficacy of our self-adjunct graph convolutional networks in overcoming the over-blurring influence of deep graph neural networks.

Researchers conducted a search for novel shadow particles linked to a leptonically decaying Z boson in proton-proton interactions at the LHC with energies of 13 TeV. This investigation involved analyzing the decay products from ZZ events where both Z bosons decayed into opposite-sign electron and muon pairs. The experiment used a data set corresponding to 36.3 fb^-1 of recorded interactions at the ATLAS detector. In the absence of the predicted signals, exclusion limits were set and compared with theoretical models, yielding thresholds for particles with masses ranging from 2 to 4.5 TeV depending on the coupling strength of 0.1 or 0.5 respectively according to a gauge-mediated supersymmetry model, with the maximum mass reach occurring at a coupling strength of 0.

A space with a specific type of structure, known as a'space with stockings', has its open sets defined not just by a subspace topology, but also includes open sets that'surround certain compact subsets'. This paper develops the theory of extended colimits within the category of spaces with'socketted open sets', showing that the universal property of the extended colimit can be used to create the'socketted topology', thereby enabling the construction of the colimit in this specific category from colimits in standard topological groups. This theory has several significant applications, particularly to uniform spaces and locally convex topological vector spaces with their bohr topologies. This final paper in a series provides the solution to an open problem initially proposed in 'Locally compact Hausdorff groups as bohr compactifications of discrete groups', published in Proc. London Math. Soc. (3) 34 (1977), 473-496.

In epitaxial growth, carbon interfaces have been instrumental in enabling the technique for a wide range of materials, yet its mechanisms remain poorly understood. Specifically, the interfaces formed between oxides and materials like rutile TiO2 exhibit weak interactions, characterized by low lattice mismatch but poor commensurability. To address this challenge, researchers introduced the concept of pinhole epitaxy, which involves a hybrid interface composed of oxid and carbon elements, thus combining strong interactions with a common crystallographic reference. Employing a combination of advanced simulations and experiments, this research investigates the equilibrium conditions of Heusler compounds grown across a graphene/sapphire interface, revealing that carbon and oxygen compete for dominance, resulting in a interface composed of both elements, thus combining pinhole and van der Waals characteristics.

This study focuses on developing a flexible and distributionally robust framework for analyzing time series with robust tails, which protects against heavy-tailed errors. It establishes key results on the convergence and weak convergence of a deterministic limiting object under minimal conditions. Based on this robust framework, it establishes consistent estimators and hypothesis testing procedures that remain reliable under various limiting scenarios. It demonstrates that these developments have broad practical applications by providing examples and proving that its findings are applicable in several important cases.

The initial red supergiant star, located at an estimated distance of 16.6 billion years (z = 3.40 +/- 0.02), is part of the gravitational lensing field of EL Gordo (ACT-CL J0102-4915), a rich cluster discovered several years ago. This star, part of the JWST PEARLS project, is one of the oldest and most distant red supergiant stars ever discovered, providing valuable insights into the universe's expansion history. Its large magnification factor, enhanced through the use of JWST's high-resolution capabilities, allows for an accurate determination of its position and, subsequently, its physical properties. This discovery represents a significant milestone in the study of lensed objects and red supergiant stars, contributing to our understanding of the universe's history and the star's estimated birth rate.

They demonstrated that the algebraic approach and the axiomatic approach are, in a broad sense, equivalent. This connection is an instance of a more general relationship between two categories, a relationship that is often referred to as a Galois-like correspondence. The $\alpha$-attractor model class, initially proposed by Kallosh et al. in 2014 for supergravity and later extended to string theory by Halverson et al. in 2018, has significant implications for inflationary cosmology and dark matter. This review focuses on various frameworks of the $\alpha$-attractor models, both in supergravity and string theory, and their resulting forecasts for dark sector particles.

Consider a quasi-Fuchsian structure with complete affine images of circular pattern, and for a given circular pattern, we explore its possible extensions to the region at infinity and evaluate all such extensions while fixing the orisphere geometry. It's proven that there are only three distinct ways a circular pattern can extend to the region at infinity while preserving the Fuchsian structure's orientation, and these extensions can be continuously varied for any given quasi-Fuchsian structure. Furthermore, it can be shown that there exists at least one unique quasi-Fuchsian structure with foliated, completely flat affine images at infinity for each given circular pattern, and this result holds regardless of the circular pattern's configuration, including interlaced configurations.

This research introduces a novel yield dispersion measure, \dys, applicable to any yield curve yield sequence. The primary goal of \dys is to assess the size of the trading range for a portfolio's yields. The size of \dys can also be used to quantify yields' predictability. The theoretical predictions are then tested using a yield portfolio strategy that adjusts a long years duration strategy by the \dys of yields, resulting in data-backed evidence that our model outperforms traditional strategies.

Effective medical diagnosis depends on accurate detection of abnormal heart sounds, 
which can be identified through advanced technology known as smartphones-based medical sensors. 
However, the presence of additional heart sounds may interfere with the detection of a specific sound 
phase, leading to difficulties in smart phone-based sound detection. 
To overcome this limitation, we developed an effective sound detection algorithm that uses a cardiac sequence alignment method.
The algorithm, which we term Cardinality-based Heart Sound Alignment (CHSA), detects all instances of a specific sound phase and ensures their consistency in duration. 
We evaluated CHSA by applying it to sound data collected from smart phones and found that it led to improved accuracy in heart sound classification compared to conventional methods. 
CHSA was also capable of handling the challenges posed by the aforementioned smartphone-based sensor, 
demonstrating its effectiveness and reliability in practical medical applications.

A twist of an affine variety X by an element g in a finite group G creates a quotient variety denoted as Xg. In this study, we examine twists of the torus by the 2-Dimensional Crystallographic Vertex Groups, which include trihedral, rhombic, and tetrahedral, octahedral, and cubic groups. We calculate the cohomology of these twist quotients, assuming X is a free torus. Furthermore, we determine the equivariant cohomology for the cases where G is a trihedral, octahedral, or cubic group, using the fact that G can be represented as subgroups in SL(3,C).

To examine the impact of social and climatic factors on economic development, we re-evaluate historical trends in industrialization by analyzing a comprehensive dataset of all countries' memberships in major international organizations spanning from 1870 to 2007. Our analysis indicates that both social climate and economic progress have intricate relationships. In particular, we found that both institutional frameworks and natural environments play a crucial role in shaping economies and developing societies. Furthermore, both institutional quality and climatic conditions significantly contribute to industrialization and economic advancement. Notably, our findings contradict the hypothesis that climate has caused institutions, and rather both are independently determined by genetic factors.

This paper examines the boundedness of a family of linear operators, a type of sequence operator associated with the fractional partial differential equation, acting between discrete Hardy spaces $H^1(\mathbb{Z}^n)$ and $H^1(\ell^p(\mathbb{Z}^n))$ for $1 < p < \infty$. It also investigates the weak type (1,1) boundedness of this family of operators and its pointwise convergence at almost every element in $\mathbb{Z}^n$.

A recent study revealed that second-price auctions, rather than first-price auctions, maintain bids closer to their true valuations due to underlying incentive structures. Building upon this discovery, our research provides the first experimental evidence showing that second-price auctions are perceived as more honest and trustworthy. In a controlled study, participants valuing transparency engaged in second-price auctions for a public good, where they consistently submitted valuations close to their true worth. A subsequent survey indicated that these participants viewed second-price auctions as more truthful compared to first-price auctions. From a practical standpoint, our findings suggest organizers should prioritize second-price auctions to encourage bid honesty.

The mechanism by which the universe transitioned from an initial state of chaos to a highly isotropic state remains one of the most intriguing problems in cosmology. To address this problem, researchers have proposed a new gravitational theory called $f(Q)$-gravity, where the quasi-symmetric scalar $Q$ forms the foundation of the theory's field equations. By assuming the existence of a barotropic fluid with monotonic density, where the pressure is directly proportional to the density, researchers were able to demonstrate that the universe's future evolution will be characterized by isotropy under a broad range of conditions. Specifically, they found that the universe's anisotropic decay rate is greater than its expansion rate and that certain constraints must be met for this to occur. Additionally, they showed that $Q$ is negative, contradicting the theory's original constraints, and that a wide range of $f(Q)$-gravity theories can lead to a universe's isotropic state regardless of the fluid's equation of state.

Hessenberg varieties, specifically the regular nilpotent Hessenberg variety, serve as a significant submanifold of flag manifold with extensive connections to algebraic combinatorics and theoretical physics. When considering a particular type of Hessenberg variety, it can be described using a specific geometric topology defined by a regular nilpotent Hessenberg function. In investigating this variety, this work employs a sophisticated mathematical tool called Gr\"obner systems to determine an advanced partition of geometric vertices, which facilitates the construction of a Gr\"obner system via the Clarke-Sturmfels algorithm. This advanced partition, which outperforms more traditional partitions such as the Bott-Samelson and Schubert partition in terms of computational efficiency, allows for a parametric Gr\"obner system to be established by analyzing the defining equations of each geometric vertex. Leveraging a specific combinatorial object called Frobenius separations, which efficiently represents geometric vertices for this particular Hessenberg variety, this advanced partition can be gr\"obnerized in an order determined by a simplified distance based on object size. This work not only demonstrates the potential of exploring geometric topology through Gr\"obner systems but also highlights an emerging field at the intersection of algebraic geometry and combinatorics that may yield novel insights into more general varieties.

The surge in neural network applications across various domains has made them a staple tool for researchers and a source of intrigue for the general public as well. Notably, the art generated or enhanced by neural networks has gained considerable attention, prompting even more interest. This document seeks to convey the enthusiasm for exploring and applying artistic elements of neural networks in creating beautiful visual masterpieces, as well as his personal experiences in this area. It seeks to serve as a guide for individuals who wish to engage with generative neural networks and transfer learning to produce or modify existing artworks, utilizing tools like GANMatic, NGAN, StyleGAN-PyTorch, PyTorch-Segmentation, and COCO-Segmentation, as well as discussing the prospects of using neural networks in art therapy.

This paper presents a dataset, known as QuRe, which is a knowledge graph constructed through the analysis of academic research papers. It answers inquiry questions from students who are learning research through their courses. To answer these questions, we utilized existing datasets, including Wikipedia, as many of the requested information could be found on it. As such, a portion of the graph is derived from an automated process that maps the required information to the corresponding Wikipedia entries. Our paper describes the construction of the knowledge graph and its source, as well as the evaluation results which show the effectiveness of the proposed approach. A preview of the graph is available for download at the following link: https://github.com/QuRe/QuRe/releases/v1.0.0

In three-dimensional core-collapse supernova simulations, rapid neutrino flavor transformations occur more frequently than previously predicted, primarily at the boundary between the standing wave and the outgoing shock in the protoneutron star. The amplitudes of these transformations peak around this region, primarily due to the significant variations in the spectral shapes of neutrinos from different regions. The chemical composition of the outgoing leptonized region also plays a key role in these transformations, with muon content significantly impacting their development. Furthermore, at high densities within the protoneutron star, neutrino oscillations rapidly switch between different types, primarily involving electron neutrinos and antineutrinos.

ADHD, a highly prevalent neurodevelopmental disorder, is often diagnosed using MRI scans and requires accurate identification of critical brain regions. Traditionally, diagnosing ADHD involves searching for patterns of hyperactive areas in the brain. However, our research challenges this perspective, demonstrating through a large-scale fMRI dataset analysis on 300 ADHD and 300 control subjects that we can effectively identify important brain areas when considering the entire brain. A novel deep learning method, which treats MRI analysis as an image classification task, classifies regions as control or ADHD, allowing us to focus on control-like regions to classify ADHD subjects. Our study reveals that crucial regions for ADHD diagnosis are located in the parietal and temporal lobes, and we find that deep learning models perform better than traditional support vector machine models when trained on these critical regions. Our findings indicate that deep learning models can be trained on ADHD-relevant regions in the brain to accurately diagnose the condition.

This study develops a theoretical framework, referred to as distinct-time SISI, to model epidemic spread by precisely defining the transition probability of infection at discrete time intervals and deriving the governing evolution equation for the infection probability. The distinct-time SISI framework is then applied to a variety of network structures, including a complete network, a homogenous Poisson network, and various non-homogenous Poisson networks characterized by specified node and link weight distributions. The analysis in this study may also be applicable to the propagation of distinct information on various network types.

This work introduces a novel service, dubbed MadDog, designed to detect and explain abbreviations within digital communications. The authors provide an extensive collection of 1,039 technical and 458 general-purpose abbreviations from various online sources. Additionally, the research involves the annotation of a substantial corpus of 6 million Twitter messages, specifically 20,000 posts, to showcase their annotations. Furthermore, the introduction of a new dataset of 1,481,537 email messages, 858 chat transcripts, 458 technical abbreviations, and 858 non-typical abbreviations completes the study's data resources. Lastly, the study presents a functional web interface for acronym detection and the development of a predictive model for acronym recognition that outperformed various existing models in a competition hosted by the Association for Computational Linguistics.

Our research reveals the possibility of dynamically switching the heat-conducting properties of quantum Hall edge states controlled by interference patterns. In a carefully designed coherent heat engine, our findings show the creation of near-perfect heat diodes that control the flow of heat and electric current. The concept of using interference to manipulate and rectify heat showcases the significant impact of phase-controlled phenomena on thermoelectric devices based on quantum Hall edges.

Recent advancements in DNA-based storage technology have made significant strides in achieving high capacity, data security, and compact spatial distribution. However, its widespread application is hindered by complex and expensive editing processes. To address this issue, our research focuses on efficiently supporting hierarchical structures and information updates within a DNA-storage system. The proposed method leverages the DNA-storage framework's capabilities to minimize changes required in the underlying model, thus reducing editing operations. The effectiveness of our approach is demonstrated through simulation results, showing substantial improvements over traditional methods in both hierarchy adjustments and data updates, specifically a 90% decrease in required editing processes.

High-energy physics researchers have made significant progress in understanding and creating various properties of topological systems and exotic quasiparticles through the control of nodal surfaces within momentum space. To help researchers study these properties of nodal surface in a tangible way, an innovative technique has been developed to create these properties in momentum space using photonic lattices, facilitating an easier observation of their characteristics through spatial measurements. This review article provides a comprehensive overview of photonic realizations of nodal surfaces in momentum space, along with an examination of topological characteristics of nodal lines and points, as well as the Nernst effect and various other phenomena associated with photonic nodal surface systems.

This study offers fresh analytical predictions for the velocity of oscillation-pattern generating waves, arising from the interaction between a stationary pacemaker zone and a moving wavefront, within the context of the FitzHugh-Nagumo system. It also provides a method to determine the critical parameter value at which the pacemaker-initiated wave velocity can be precisely calculated as the wavefront approaches the pacemaker zone. These results are supplemented by relevant literature that proposes alternative approaches to this problem.

Approximating the von Neumann entropy of a quantum state is a fundamental objective in both theoretical and practical applications. However, the current best method achieves this approximation in O(d^2) time, where d is the dimension of the state, limiting its applicability. Our research proposes two random sampling-based methods for estimating the entropy of a known quantum state $\rho$ with O(d^2/r) and optimal O(d^{\frac{7}{3}}/r) quantum query complexities, where r is the number of samples of $\rho$ that a quantum algorithm can prepare efficiently. When r scales as O(d^2), our algorithm outperforms existing methods by a factor of d^0.55. Additionally, we develop a method for extracting the entropy of the reduced state from purifications of $\rho$ in O(d^{\frac{7}{3}}/r) time. Our results also include proving the inapproximability of the entropy for certain states and demonstrating the inapproximability of the mutual information between the subsystems in the uniform superposition state in reduced state.

The increasing reliance on artificial intelligence (AI) in medical imaging is evident, 
with its capabilities in enhancing diagnostic accuracy and streamlining clinical operations. 
Nonetheless, the clinical implementation of AI is hindered by several technical obstacles, 
including data management and infrastructure utilization. 
This study delves into the computational demands of AI model training, highlighting effective data management strategies that reduce computational overheads. 
Specifically, it highlights the role of advanced data management systems in optimizing training processes and hampers the clinical deployment of AI by highlighting the need for efficient data management systems and optimal cloud infrastructure. 
To address these challenges, we present our experience in developing a unified AI platform that integrates AI model development, deployment, and monitoring. 
This platform aims to streamline the AI workflow, enhance collaboration among data scientists and clinicians, and facilitate the adoption of AI in medical imaging.

This study proposes an innovative, semi-supervised automated ICD coding system, using NLP techniques to identify diagnosis codes from electronic health records without requiring extensive manual coding of entire datasets. To address data sparsity, the model incorporates an embedded topic model and leverages relevant patient information found in diagnostic descriptions and metadata. In comparison to a fully supervised baseline model, the semi-supervised approach demonstrates comparable performance, with significant improvements in precision, recall, and overall accuracy observed for certain ICD categories. In contrast to another semi-supervised method, the proposed model outperforms in computational speed and produces more accurate and precise results, indicating its potential to improve real-world clinical operations.

A breakthrough in monitoring quantum systems has been made, allowing for the closed-loop measurement and analysis of complex states known as spin cat states. This loop is completed by quantum algorithmic operations that are automatically adjusted based on the measured outcomes. We have successfully implemented this process on a superconducting quantum processor built by TRION Technology, using a two-qubit trapdoor tunnel junction (TTJ) quantum circuit to generate the desired states and implement feedback operations. Our research extends beyond experimental achievements, including the theoretical development of a quantum algorithm capable of learning maximum-likelihood parameters in systems that can be monitored, as well as the design of these states on alternative quantum hardware.

This gravitational phenomenon occurs when one star passes in front of another, causing it to appear larger than normal for a short period. Researchers have used KMTNet data to identify various transient phenomena, including binary systems, relativistic effects, and other anomalies. Specifically, this study presents a comprehensive collection of 54 celestial anomalies, observed in the 2018 prime-field by KMTNet team members.
