A key challenge in solving inverse problems lies in determining the object or scene configuration that best matches the observed shadows cast by a scene. Our research focuses on developing an effective method for computing shadows in four dimensions, accounting for the x, y, z, and time coordinates. By employing differentiable ray casting using static geometry, we present a fully differentiable method for computing shadows, facilitating the use of backpropagation to solve four-dimensional shadow inverse problems. Through end-to-end backpropagation, we can accurately reconstruct scenes from shadow data, an task typically intractable. By integrating our method with modern rendering techniques, we demonstrate that it supports various types of observations and is applicable to various image restoration tasks. Our approach proves particularly valuable in solving four-dimensional shadow inverse problems, such as reconstructing scenes from temporal images.

Stochastic origin-destination demand estimation is crucial for real-time traffic management and prediction. However, accurately estimating this demand using traffic flow data remains a significant challenge. This paper develops and evaluates multiple statistical estimators for stochastic OD demand using full-day traffic flow information collected at sensors on routes between OD pairs. An entropy-based estimator and generalized method of moments estimators are among the methods considered, each employing different approaches to utilize available traffic data. To facilitate comparison and understanding of the models' accuracy, we also introduce alternative OD demand alternatives that respect the constraints imposed by traffic flow and probability theory. These solutions can be formulated as convex optimization problems under certain assumptions. To further assess and rank the estimators, we develop metrics for measuring their accuracy and efficiency, including relative bias and relative efficiency. Our analysis utilizes a small-scale network with known stochastic OD demands and corresponding traffic flow data to simulate and test the estimators. Our results show that an estimator utilizing full-day traffic data and based on the method of moments outperforms other alternatives, including an existing method of moments estimator utilizing complete traffic data, in terms of relative efficiency and accuracy.

In a system composed of multiple identical oscillators with identical connections, we demonstrate that multiple stable states of synchronized oscillation exist, each corresponding to a distinct combination of oscillation frequencies, and that their relative likelihoods can be determined by a criterion based on their spectral properties. Furthermore, it is possible that the amplitude properties of these synchronized states can be directly inferred from the global eigenmodes of the system's connectivity matrix. Our findings also reveal that in systems where parameters are slightly variable, the combination of this diversity and linear relationships among the eigenvectors of the system's connectivity matrix gives rise to complex synchronization patterns, including multiple simultaneous synchronized states, oscillations that are collectively coherent yet individually distinct, and more.

The ABR and W algorithms generate uniform spanning trees through random walks; ABR utilizes a single infinite random walk, while W employs a series of potentially infinite random walks. In contrast, it has been demonstrated that an alteration of the ABR process can temporarily mimic one phase of W, specifically up to the point when the algorithm has discovered the farthest node from the starting point of the walk. Due to their disparate complexities, which are respectively $O(m)$ and $O(m/n \cdot \text{mix})$, where $m$ represents edges, $n$ represents vertices, and mix represents the mixing time, ABR and W have been used for varying graph sizes; however, it has been discovered that one modified version of the ABR process, limited to the farthest node, can temporarily mimic one phase of W, specifically up to the point when the algorithm has discovered the farthest node from the starting point of the walk, since the two processes share no commonality beyond this point. As a direct result, it has been possible to combine the strengths of both algorithms into a two-phase framework for generating uniform spanning trees, taking only $O(\max(\text{far}, \text{mix}))$ expected work, where far represents the far expected work.

Recent advances in unified multimodal representation learning have inspired researchers to integrate diverse data types, like sheet music and audio, into a single model. However, there has been a lack of a comprehensive music dataset that combines both modalities, hindering the development of effective music AI systems. Introducing a music dataset termed MusicTM-Dataset featuring about 1,000 samples that seamlessly combine sheet music, lyrics, and audio, can promote innovative thinking in the music AI field and promote cultural preservation through music. This music dataset is thoroughly described in this work, highlighting its distinctive characteristics, including a novel sheet music representation called music tokens. These music tokens are generated using a sheet music transformer that can output music tokens matching individual musical measures, enabling enhanced accuracy in music IAM inference tasks and facilitating more precise input music token generation for downstream tasks like IAM denoising and IAM score generation. This work also presents a Music/Text LLM, resulting in a highly accurate sheet music generation system that produces music tokens instead of raw musical notes, leading to more realistic music tokens and more accurate IAM denoising performance compared to prior state-of-the-art models.

This research focuses on a comparative analysis of two popular knowledge graphs, Ontodia and Wikidata, to understand the impact of their respective embeddings on data analytics and machine learning applications. By utilizing knowledge graphs that incorporate natural language labels, various properties, and relationships, data models can achieve enhanced results, including the use of network flow and community detection algorithms. The findings derived from experiments employing the PowerFlow, Yifan, and Lear algorithms on the Wikidata dataset illustrate superior performance compared to a previous study utilizing a knowledge graph of computer networks, thereby underscoring the versatility of entities within knowledge graphs.

The impact of a spatially varying refractive index on dark solitons is investigated in this study, where an exact analytical method is used to derive the linear stability of the results. Finding that a modulated linear dispersion effect influences dark solitons in a different way compared to other nonlinearity effects, a numerical approach via the Fourier transform variational technique was employed to derive the approximation of the stability. The findings demonstrate that dark solitons can remain stable and oscillate in presence of the modulated linear dispersion effect, where their amplitude and phase dynamics can be explained by an analytical approximation method.

We present a novel framework, called Lotse, for computer-assisted tasks in visual analysis. Lotse empowers users to seamlessly integrate and manage assistance elements like related metadata, automatic patterns, and functional tools, all within a unified and dynamic environment that adapts to user interactions. Built on Python's powerful capabilities, Lotse leverages the D3 library to ensure performance, relatedness, and context-awareness of assistance built-ins. This paper delves into the rationale behind Lotse's architecture, its defining characteristics, and a prototype implementation, while also highlighting its potential for enhancing user-supported interactions in visual analysis.

Designing a stellarator relies heavily on meticulously engineered twisted coils called poloidal field coils. These coils generate the required magnetic fields to confine the plasma within the device. Due to their intricate shape and proximity to each other, these coils experience significant electrical forces that can make their support structure and motorized adjustment system withstand stress. Virtual testing using digital twins allows us to evaluate and optimize the design before physical construction begins. This paper explores the potential of replacing some of these coils with permanently magnetized coilless segments and reconfiguring the remaining coils to maintain the same plasma confinement while reducing stresses on the remaining components. By reconfiguring the coils, we can improve the overall efficiency and cost-effectiveness of the stellarator design, particularly in devices like the National Ignition Facility where D. Spong is the primary author, along with contributions from J. Boice, J. DeGrassi, A. Wootton, A. Weygand, and C. Kellman. By analyzing the magnetic field requirements and optimizing coil configurations, we can achieve a new equilibrium configuration that maintains the same plasma confinement as the original design. This is achieved by adjusting current in selected coils and ensuring the plasma remains in a stable and efficient confinement state. This process can be carried out using a custom-written code called PINTA and verified with finite element analysis, showing a potential 30% reduction in the maximum coil forces experienced and demonstrating the feasibility of integrating coilless segments into the stellarator design.

Our research involves using an advanced imaging technique, specifically T2-weighted MRI, to analyze how heat is distributed in a stationary bed of particles. To accomplish this, we developed a special sample holder that enables real-time monitoring of heat within the bed by using a rapid data acquisition method of about 1 second. The study specifically examined the thermal behavior of stationary beds of glass beads and pelleted catalyst particles, and we found that the T2 relaxation time plays a crucial role in interpreting heat transfer patterns, particularly when the particle size is very small and interstitial fluid temperatures are in equilibrium with the particles. Moreover, the use of an inverse heat conduction model, which takes into account the finite time for data collection in MRI, has successfully allowed us to reconstruct heat maps and determine the heating and cooling patterns of particles in the bed, and this model's predictive capabilities were validated through the use of particle image velocimetry to assess the fluid flow dynamics within the bed.

The dynamic behavior of self-assembling macromolecules is a vital aspect to consider for understanding the fundamental processes underpinning life's essential functions. Recent research has demonstrated that macromolecules adhere to a universal set of principles, which enables their predictable behavior. In the field of drug development, the macromolecular element known as beta-sheets, associated with macromolecular malfunctions, has gained significant attention. A recent study found that certain peptides exhibiting different organizational patterns can still incorporate into the same type of fiber or crystal structure. To explore this phenomenon, our team employed a mean-field-based approach to investigate how universal principles govern the behavior of interacting macromolecules, which can form two distinct types of fibers or crystals. Specifically, our model explores how a mixture of two types of macromolecules, which have no direct interaction, still exhibits a wide range of possible outcomes, including the exclusive formation of one type, the other, or both in an alternating or stable coexistence pattern. In an alternating pattern, one type of macromolecule binds to its counterpart before they self-assemble into a fiber or crystal. In the stable coexistence pattern, both types of macromolecule bind to each other, but then only one type self-assembles into a fiber or crystal.

This study provides the first in-depth analysis of a major solar flare and CME eruption associated with a coronal mass ejection from a sunspot on the solar disk's edge during a solar storm on the back of a large, complex magnetic field area on the Sun. Utilizing high-resolution images from the High-Resolution Coronal Imaging System and data from other instruments, researchers were able to observe a significant disturbance in magnetic field lines caused by a rotating sunspot, leading to the coronal mass ejection. This observation corroborates previous studies on solar flare and CME phenomena, revealing that the rotation of a solar area can play a crucial role in triggering such events.

This note builds on the M. Wolf's b-theorem, which is an extension of the Maslov index. It is a condition that ensures a certain integrality for the Maslov form when modulated by the B-field, thus defining the elements of the 2nd torsion cohomology group. It is proposed that the b-theorem is a consequence of a more fundamental principle - the F-theorem - which posits that the Maslov form should be representable as a smooth form square of the Hamiltonian vector field. The B-field vector potential, in turn, should be represented as a smooth 1-form. The present b-theorem is seen to be susceptible to counterexamples due to its attempt to enforce differentiability of the 1-form associated with the Maslov vector field, which is not necessarily differentiable, for symplectic manifolds with boundary. The problem can be circumvented by considering an equivariant version of the Maslov vector field, which is valid for all closed manifolds and which has an equivariant version of the Maslov form - the equivariant Maslov form, which is seen to be cohomologically equivalent to the Maslov form when the boundary is present. The existing version of the b-theorem is seen to be susceptible to the potential of the 1-form, which is seen to be susceptible to a potential 1-form, which is seen to be susceptible to the potential of the Maslov form, which is seen to be susceptible

This research investigates various multilevel algorithms for solving cardiac tissue displacement fields from regional stress equilibrium equations, which are typically difficult due to complex material properties and smoothness constraints, resulting in a highly ill-conditioned problem that hinders the convergence of standard iterative solvers. Several multilevel algorithms with specialized preconditioners such as block diagonal, block Hilbert-Schmidt, and algebraic multigrid methods are compared to determine the most effective approach. These algorithms utilize scalable implicit solvers for fine level corrections, including finite element, finite difference, and spectral element discretizations, and the study finds that the block Hilbert-Schmidt multilevel algorithm to be the most robust and efficient approach.

The analysis of tag usage patterns in social tagging systems offers valuable insights into user behavior, system evolution, user interest trends, user collaboration dynamics, system interest exchange mechanisms, and system of use cases. To this end, we introduce a conceptual framework that quantifies collaboration and interest metrics based on user behavior such as reuse, time-based dynamics, and information flow. This framework is then applied to two major social tagging systems, Del.icio.us and Flickr, using a comprehensive dataset of nearly 23 million tags, to compute both intra-user and inter-user collaboration measures, as well as measures of user interest in tags, tag sets, and users. Empirical results show that our proposed measures effectively identify and distinguish instances of collaboration, interest exchange, use cases, and interest dynamics within these systems.

Micro-fabricated metagratings created at acoustic epitaxy temperatures have the potential to control and manipulate acoustic waves in new ways. By incorporating very shallow scatterers in a metagrating structure, it becomes possible to significantly reduce its thickness, thereby enhancing its ability to concentrate acoustic energy and improving its functionality as a heat-conducting device or a complex acoustic system. Using advanced two-photon lithography technology, researchers have successfully created complex metagrating structures with features as small as 100 micrometers, capable of efficiently manipulating ultrasonic waves in the 2-20 MHz frequency range with minimal insertion loss.

We investigate the long-term behavior of the two-dimensional compressible FENE dumbbell model, an extension of the Navier-Stokes equations that incorporates a dumbbell model for closure, particularly focusing on its robust solution properties. It is established that, given initial values within a specific, two-dimensional, function space that accommodates both large oscillations and small energies, the resulting global weak solution is unique and exhibits exponential decay as time progresses. This finding is supported by an approach that involves precise estimates of the solution and its associated Fourier transform.

Cellular networks known as Integrated Access and Backhaul (IAB) use the radio frequency to create integrated and self-contained networks that can be rapidly deployed in situations requiring significant bandwidth, such as large events and natural disasters. While stationary IAB networks have shown great potential, deploying mobile IAB networks to meet these demands remains an unresolved issue. This work explores the possibilities and challenges of implementing mobile IAB networks and suggests possible approaches to make them a reality.

In this research, two formal methodologies for hyperparameter in evolutionary algorithms are examined through two distinct methods: the Sobol and the PERS, leading to the identification of key variables and their impact on the outcomes. Both methods confirm that population size and mutation strength are the most significant EA variables, while the choice of variation operator is also significant according to the Sobol method. Furthermore, the analysis reveals that certain EA and GA function evaluations and generations are also important for determining ranking efficiency. Additionally, the results enable the creation of an informed starting configuration for hyperparameters, namely strong mutation strength and a sufficiently large population size, which allows the EA to effectively explore the search area and efficiently find high-ranking solutions.

The paper utilizes wave function behavior at boundaries to demonstrate the equivalence of operators $-\Delta$ and $-{\Delta}_{\Gamma}$ on a specific domain of functions, which leads to the transformation of the time-dependent Schrödinger equation with the Laplacian into two linked equations describing a quantum wave and its boundary wave. The study also examines the implications of this transformation on the energy and energy density of the system.

As evaluation of reinforcement learning (RL) techniques becomes increasingly crucial in academic research, the scarcity of comprehensive evaluation frameworks and libraries in RL has become a pressing issue. To address this gap, we introduce L2Explorer, a web-based platform that facilitates the continuous evaluation of RL methods through an extensive collection of environments, metrics, and evaluation techniques. Comprising 22 operational evaluators, 12 development-stage evaluators, and 70 operational environments, L2Explorer can simultaneously test a vast number of methods across a diverse range of environments, enabling thorough, reproducible, and in-depth analysis of RL techniques. Furthermore, we evaluate state-of-the-art methods on a selected collection of tasks within our framework and analyze their relative strengths, limitations, and areas for improvement. The comprehensive documentation accompanying our system serves as a thorough guide for users and provides additional insight into RL technique evaluation in general. The complete L2Explorer system, accompanied by extensive documentation and a reproducible analysis of RL methods, may be accessed at https://explorer.l2abc.com/.

The Liger instrument at the W. M. Keck Observatory, designed for Near-Infrared Low-resolution Integral Field Spectroscopy, has undergone installation and initial testing since late 2022. This paper outlines the design and implementation of the data processing system, data flow, and software interfaces for the Liger experiment at the Keck Observatory. Specifically, the study focuses on the Kepler experiment's infrastructure as a reference for higher-level software connections and the Liger instrument's specific software links, including the instrument control system, the camera's data acquisition and synchronization system, and the guiding system.

This study focuses on the 2D incompressible Navier-Stokes equation, revealing the long-term (as $t\to+\infty$) and short-term ($t\to 0$) dynamics of solutions near a traveling wave that's a modified version of the Couette flow solution to the Euler equation. The global asymptotic behavior of initially close solutions to the Couette flow has been proven, with the connection to the original wave or a shifted/multiple version of it. The local asymptotic behavior is also studied, with the rate of convergence determined by the initial data through the use of a space-time weighted norm.

We investigated the optical control of polarized light using a single and an integrated cavity with exciton-polariton condensates. In the case of a single cavity, we observed an optical control of the polarized light properties through a control beam interacting with a weak probe beam, resulting in a significant change in the probe beam's polarizability when the system transitions from a polarized superfluid to a polarized Mott insulator state. Furthermore, we demonstrated a control of both the polarizability and phase of the probe beam in a integrated cavity system, where the two cavities are weakly connected by an integrated mirror. In this setup we observed changes in the polarizability and phase of the probe beam as a function of the polarized beam density when the system transitions through a polarized condensate interference pattern. In addition, we observed modifications in the polarizability and phase match conditions when the system is in a periodic potential potential potential potential potential.

This study is set to deterministic, stochastic versions of the KPZ equation where a key component - a nonlocal 'slope term,' is used to model interface growth. We demonstrate that in deterministic form, this equation can be solved in $2$ and higher dimensions when the 'slope term' is modeled by a Cauchy process with varying speed, a finding that extends to fractional Laplacians in some cases. In stochastic versions, we establish that for a specific type of noise and 'slope term,' solutions in $2$ dimensions are well-defined and even in all fractional cases are well-defined up to a certain temporal limit in all $d$ dimensions. Interestingly, when the 'slope term' is made up of a Cauchy process with varying speed, a weak solution can be obtained in all $d$ dimensions. Furthermore, we have found that when this key component - a Cauchy process with varying speed, is set to zero, a well-known variant of the stochastic Burgers equation can be found in all $d$ dimensions.

In the midst of the COVID-19 pandemic, governments around the world have to make crucial public health decisions with limited information to protect their populations. This paper delves into the forecasting models of COVID-19 in South Africa, a medium-income country with a highly unequal distribution of healthcare resources and a substantial informal sector. These unique characteristics have led to an accelerated and intense transmission of the virus in certain areas, particularly in the city of Johannesburg. Utilizing the available data on confirmed cases and incorporating the principles of SIR-based epidemiological modeling, our research forecasts the pandemic's trajectory in South Africa. According to our predictions, peak infection rates are expected to be reached within a few weeks, at which point healthcare systems may become overwhelmed and a substantial portion of the population could be infected. This analysis underscores the critical need for widespread testing and a clear, unified public health strategy to effectively manage the pandemic.

Freiman's 3k-4 conjecture has long held that any subset of an abelian group, containing at least four elements and a sumset of cardinality 2k-1 or less, has a cardinality no greater than that of a specific structure called nearly arithmetic progressions. We have found that this property also applies to subsets of non-abelian groups, but with a slightly higher upper bound on cardinality. Specifically, if the cardinality of the sumset is between $(\frac{7}{3} + \epsilon)k$ and $2k-1$, then the subset has a cardinality of at most that of the near-AP in a non-abelian group.

Ophthalmic imaging is crucial in detecting and monitoring eye diseases, and recent research has focused on using artificial intelligence to analyze retinal images. One challenge involves handling the large amount of data from different imaging modalities. This study addresses this challenge with a novel method of multimodal data fusion for detecting 3 stages of diabetic retinopathy and 2 levels of glaucoma from multiple retinal image sources. The proposed approach uses a neural network to identify common and unique features from different retinal images, and then combines this information in two ways: using the attention mechanism to prioritize important input and simply combining the inputs at the classification stage. Both proposed architectures achieved high accuracy in categorizing retinal images, and the study found that using attention-based fusion performed better than combining inputs at the classification stage for certain conditions. Additionally, the study found that fusing multiple retinal image sources consistently improved performance over using single sources for both diseases.

To mitigate the COVID-19 pandemic's impact, accurate and efficient diagnosis of patients is crucial. X-ray imaging has gained significant attention due to its safety, speed, and cost-effectiveness. Our analysis of the X-ray images of COVID-19 patients revealed distinct features in specific lung regions, in particular the lower lungs. Given that Intensive Care Unit (ICU) admission is characterized by severe symptoms, particularly visible in the lower lungs, we propose that the degree of infection in these regions may serve as an indicator for potential ICU treatment requirements. Our findings also suggest that additional research is required to validate this hypothesis and refine it for clinical application.

This study presents novel analytical techniques to derive boundary information from the squared transmission eigenvalues and associated functions of a given optical medium, akin to the well-known Wigner delay time, but with broader applicability including beyond the low-energy regime. The presented methods include formulas for calculating transmission zeros, eigenvalues, and partial boundary phase profiles. This mathematical framework is applicable to any spherically symmetric medium, regardless of its constituent material homogeneity. The research findings are subsequently validated through comparison with the media's direct transmission functions, especially in the case of an organ pipe and a Göktürk-Toscano-Zhang mirror.

To effectively grasp user intent in conversations, conversational systems rely on intent identification (II), which also benefits from fine-tuning pre-trained models. However, to enhance their performance, I propose training II models in three progressive stages: (1) leveraging language models to establish a basic model capable of identifying basic user requests, (2) employing label propagation to facilitate cross-domain learning and expand the label set, (3) utilizing comparative learning to improve model accuracy by distinguishing similar examples, while using pre-training to accelerate training and reduce overfitting. The proposed approach significantly boosts II model performance in terms of accuracy and efficiency.

The global simplicial bundle S (S (E (B))) (S (B), F) is a simple way to make a global version of the simplicial path object, which helps us understand the relationship between the simplicial structure of B and the fiber F, and is useful in the study of the homotopy of the mapping space from B to S, as well as the classifying space of a group which acts on a space, which can also be thought of as the simplicial quotient of the action space by the group which acts on it.

In group theory, counting the number of subgroups within a finite group is a common and significant task. Several methods, such as those proposed by Feit, Pyber, and Shalev, have been developed to establish clear upper limits on the total number of subgroups. This paper contributes to that goal by deriving an new upper bound on the count of subgroups in certain finite groups, effectively improving existing results and extending previous findings.

This review starts with the state-space formulation of the small-disturbance, high-energy equations and then discusses the Model Trajectory Algorithm (MTA) and its role in deriving formulas for the perturbed equations of motion. We focus on an specific formula of this type, analyzing its underlying assumptions, known limitations, empirical success rate, and the criteria for detecting trajectory collapse. Furthermore, we review existing search strategies for the formula's unknown parameters and the available solution libraries, also known as banks of control laws. Our review is based on the fundamental theory of the optimal control problem as long as the motion remains within the linear regime. Building upon this foundation, an upcoming publication addresses the development of control laws for motion beyond the linear regime.

One major challenge in Visual Association Detection (VAD), which ranks highly important image and video search tasks, lies in handling false positives effectively. A limiting factor in the current VAD system is the lack of a well-defined negative class, resulting in the model's inability to recognize erroneous detections. As such, we aim to enhance VAD by identifying and addressing false positives, by introducing a novel approach that involves detecting misidentified associations. The proposed method utilizes two key components: 1) a mechanism for locating ambiguous regions associated with erroneous detections, and 2) a module for verifying the validity of relevant visual cues to ensure they do not support incorrect associations. Our comprehensive experiments on identifying false positives in VAD have demonstrated superior performance. The proposed framework can even serve as a standalone filter to reject samples associated with erroneous detections and is applicable to various existing VAD frameworks.

The expectation cost of quantum associations in the context of weak measurements is analyzed in this paper, considering the information in quantum states that is captured by certain operators through minimal disturbance. It is demonstrated that the associated expense of this information is half as much as the post-measurement association expense. A specific scenario involving the detection of single photons via polarization is used to verify the theory's validity by calculating the expense through the actual manipulation of quantum resources.

This study addresses the task of generating a social network graph by leveraging texts that describe interpersonal relationships, employing a data-driven methodology to construct a graph where each node represents an individual and each edge signifies a relationship between two people. Unlike existing approaches that focus on specific relationship types or limited social networks, this research presents a novel model capable of capturing various relationship categories within multiple social contexts. Furthermore, this approach innovatively uses a bidirectional model to simultaneously process social network data and node information using text-based models and demonstrates that it effectively enhances the model's performance in relationship prediction and text encoding tasks. A newly created, large-scale dataset named InterpersonalNodes has been developed and made available for use, demonstrating the model's efficacy and outperforming existing social relationship prediction benchmarks.

Our novel approach, Dynamic Graph Message Transmission Networks (DGMTNs),
utilize graphs to model the relationships between image components, with the graph
structure and node connections evolving over time through sequential image subregions.
These networks can effectively capture both long- and short-term dynamics, leading to
excellent results across image, video, and audio tasks. Our DGMTN architecture excels
at learning time-dependent features and generating context-driven representations, making
it applicable to various identification tasks such as image spatial, video temporal, cross-media,
and cross-domain transfer learning. Our experiments validate DGMTNs' superior
performance on multiple image, video, cross-media, and cross-domain tasks. Our code is
accessible at https://github.com/wkent1994/DGMTN.

This paper proposes an innovative architecture for processing images, capable of efficiently handling image filtering operations, such as constant multiplication, with a focus on reducing hardware expense. Our research specifically targets the multiplication of an 8-bit number by a constant value, and we found that this operation can be executed using either two additions, one subtraction, and one shift operation, all in constant time. We made contributions in multiple areas: we developed and tested various algorithms for this purpose, created and optimized open-source tools for evaluating these algorithms, and designed a novel image processing pipeline, the NumConstMul architecture, that leverages our findings. Our results show that the NumConstMul architecture can achieve a 5.4 times speedup over conventional processors, while resulting in a 2.5 times reduction in hardware expense for executing image filtering operations, such as those used in computer vision applications.

Quantum machine learning is an emerging field that explores the possibility of leveraging quantum devices to enhance the computational capabilities of machine learning models, particularly in terms of speed and memory efficiency. It is crucial to distinguish between quantum machine learning and machine learning on quantum data, though they are intimately related. This paper will not cover all the legal and practical hurdles associated with quantum devices but rather concentrate on showcasing innovative quantum neural architectures and their associated challenges associated with training. We'll start by outlining fundamental concepts associated with quantum computing and relevant circuit designs, before delving into the specifics of quantum learning models, such as recommendation systems, regression models, and generative models. Next, we'll explore the hurdles associated with these models, particularly training difficulties such as landscape complexity, measurement errors, and data transmission limitations associated with NISQ devices, along mitigation strategies. Finally, we'll discuss emerging research directions, such as the development of hybrid and stochastic quantum models, noisy or imperfect unitary transformations, and the need to efficiently verify the quantum advantages associated with these approaches, particularly in terms of generating high-quality samples, along massive parallel training capabilities.

Radiation damage from high-energy particle beams can significantly degrade the performance of radio frequency (RF) cavities used in accelerators, causing the loss of radio frequency power and potential damage to amplifiers.  As a result, there is a growing need to develop new technologies that can efficiently boost the power of RF systems while also being resilient to radiation.  This has driven the community to explore the potential of GaN and GaAs HEMT amplifiers, as well as the development of robust and reliable power combiners.  This paper summarizes the current state of RF booster technology, highlighting recent research and testing, as well as future research and development directions.

In this review, the historical context of the muon collider is revisited, along with the current state of research into muon colliders, from initial conception to the most recent developments. Various muon collider designs are examined, including a muon-factory option and colliders with center-of-mass energies of 0.3 TeV, 1 TeV, and 3 TeV. The feasibility of the muon collider is assessed, focusing on key technical breakthroughs in muon production, focusing, and radiation shielding. Future prospects for muon colliders, particularly in the contexts of the HL-LHC and future electron colliders, are also explored.

This study applies a general mathematical technique to derive dispersion relations for relativistic Navier-Stokes hydrodynamics, then uses these results to compare with the kinetic theory of Boltzmann. We demonstrate how the relaxation time and cross-sectional properties of collisions influence sound wave and shear viscosity-driven modes in fluids with finite viscosity and thermal conductivity.

Our research investigates the potential for a significant contribution of primordial black holes (PBHs) to the background of captured and decaying dark matter (DD) and the associated flux of neutrinos from the Sun. In DD, PBHs are decaying into pairs of Z-bosons, which then decay into quark pairs. In the scenario of capture, a PBH is created at the top of the Sun and falls towards its center due to gravity. In both cases, the PBH is captured within the Sun, where its decays generate a Z-boson with an energy of around 45 GeV. This energy is comparable to the detection thresholds of neutrino telescopes such as IceCube and KM3NeT. As a result, DD can lead to a significant Z-boson flux of around 10 per year, per cubic centimeter, and 50 per year, per cubic centimeter, at the KM3NeT/OCA and IceCube-Gen2 detection thresholds respectively. Consequently, the neutrino flux may interfere with our understanding of the origin of DD.

Our focus is on developing secure multi-party computation processes that employ a hybrid approach, combining bit-security with boolean security. The complexity of bit-security based protocols makes them impractical for real-world applications due to their inefficiency. Consequently, a new approach is needed to enhance the efficiency of bit-security based protocols. The Safe Framework proposed by Roy et al. is promising, as it combines homomorphic encryption capabilities with boolean gates to increase efficiency. However, this framework has a critical flaw: it is vulnerable to specific attacks due to its reliance on an insecure comparison operation. To address this issue, we present the Virtual Safe Framework - an enhanced version of the Safe Framework - which incorporates an insecure comparison operation in a protected manner. The framework consists of a five-stage pipeline that validates and optimizes expressions before execution. Moreover, a security analysis has been carried out to assess the feasibility of the framework's optimizations. Compared to existing processes based on boolean gates and TFHE, our framework has been found to have promising potential, as demonstrated by comparative latency analysis.

We have developed an approximation scheme for a type of combinatorial optimization problem known as weighted constraint satisfaction problems. This weighted problem involves finding the most favorable configuration of variables to maximize the total weight of satisfied constraints within a given domain. For problems with a limited number of variables per constraint and a sizeable problem instance, we have proved an approximation scheme where the approximation error is related to the constant number of variables per constraint. However, if there is no upper limit on the number of constraints, this method may not yield polynomial-time approximations. In the case of strictly positive weights for constraints with two variables, we have demonstrated an efficient approximation scheme. Furthermore, we have shown an improved approximation method, valued at roughly 1.203, for positively weighted unit constraints.

often involving fine-tuning the models on downstream tasks, which requires access to various APIs and substantial computational resources. 
However, unsupervised few-shot learning methods can utilize pre-trained models more effectively by accessing them directly through APIs,

employ a common approach of testing pre-trained models through APIs and evaluating their performance on few-shot tasks by comparing the results to human annotations.
