To efficiently manage and monitor power outages in distribution networks, utility companies need reliable methods to pinpoint the occurrence of an outage within a specific geographic area. While UIOutage.com successfully tracks and maps out large-scale commercial outages, it's unclear how well this service performs during actual outages. Our research focuses on analyzing user-reported data from UIOutage.com to develop a data-driven approach for detecting outages in real-time. Our proposed method utilizes user submission patterns, user interface design, and graph-based user-reported data to accurately identify outages. Experimental outcomes demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach, showcasing an F1-score of 0.9186 in a two-class classification model and highlighting a lead time of approximately 15 minutes before traditional detection methods, such as SCADA and AMI, can identify an outage through lost phasor data measurements.

Our 2017 study on the radiative decay $X(3872)\rightarrow J/\psi \pi \gamma$ led to a contradiction with an earlier analysis of the same process due to differing estimates of the transition form factor $g_{X(3872)\rightarrow J/\psi \pi \pi}$ at high $\pi \pi$ energies. To eliminate this discrepancy, the form factor was assumed to remain constant across the entire energy spectrum. In the current work, the inconsistency is resolved by employing a straightforward dispersion relation that relates $g_{X(3872)\rightarrow J/\psi \pi \pi}$ to the wave function derivative of $X(3872)$ at its resonance position. Additionally, two additional transition form factors, related to charged counterparts of the $X(3872)$ decay process, are calculated using simple quark model estimates.

We define and analyze in section 3 "categorical quadrics" - abstract concepts representing quadratic hypersurfaces in section 4. Their existence in terms of real vector spaces is demonstrated in section 5 using a specific building block, a line bundle over Grassmannian space, which yields examples in various contexts such as symplectic and orthogonal categories, as well as Catalan number related examples.

Text-based games provide a rigorous platform to evaluate basic AI capabilities by closely mirroring real-world complexities, particularly in understanding and processing text. For a long time, text-based games have been regarded as particularly challenging for AI due to the intricate nature of language and syntax. In our study, we introduce TextWorldExpress, a text-based game simulation that operates at an unprecedented speed of one million moves per second, enabling us to demonstrate state-of-the AI capabilities in solving text-based puzzles within a very limited time frame. By optimizing our game engine and using high-performance computing strategies, we have successfully accelerated the play rate by a significant margin of at least 4 orders of magnitude compared to previous achievements. Furthermore, we present RACE, a racing competition platform for text-based games that fosters innovation and healthy competition among AI researchers by comparing different AI approaches within a specific time constraint.

To Thegeometric method to Topological Insulators is relatively well-established.
However, its application to flawed Topological Insulators presents two major obstacles:
firstly, there is a lack of clear definition for flawed Topological Insulators in the spin system model,
and secondly, traditional geometric methods rely heavily on periodicity which is compromised by impurities.
We have addressed these limitations by developing a theoretical framework that uses local sub-blocks and an updated boundary state approach,
which is suitable for systems with flaws and gives rise to the concept of local geometric quantities.
Our results indicate that this local quantity is invariant in magnitude but its sign is determined by the local topological properties of valence bands.
This concept can be effectively applied to analyze geometric properties of flawed Topological Insulators using neural networks.
To demonstrate this new method, we have successfully trained a neural network to identify geometric properties of randomly doped models of Topological Insulators.

Consider a sector $S_\gamma$ with an angle of $\gamma$ and home to the origin in the plane $\mathbb R^2$. The $p$-Neumann problem for $p$-harmonic functions with a given boundary condition of $x\mapsto |x|^{\beta}(e^{i\gamma k}P_k(x/|x|))$, where $k$ is an integer, was investigated. The function involves a polynomial $P_k$ of degree $\beta p$, where $\beta$ must be an odd integer when $p$ is even, or any positive integer if $p$ is an odd number. The function's growth or decay rate is determined as $O(|x|^{\beta p + 1})$.

This research develops novel statistical methods for estimating the joint probability of exceeding very high threshold values in multiple dimensions, taking into account a space variable, and visualizes these estimates using contour maps. We also introduce a new non-parametric method for modeling extreme events in different areas of the North Sea and the English Channel, which uses the Chapeau-Juge approach to consider seasonal variations. To validate our methods, both simulation tests and real-world数据分析 were used, demonstrating the effectiveness of our models in predicting extreme weather events in different regions and providing accurate forecasts for areas not yet studied.

Let K be a fixed number field and a fixed positive integer n. Consider a set Gni of functions, where each function f from A to B is defined such that for any point a in the affine space of dimension n over K, the value of f at a is in a finite set. We define a corresponding set Gn of functions, where each function f from A to B is defined such that for any point a in the affine space of dimension n over a fixed number field K, the value of f at a is in a finite set. We prove that the cardinality of Gni is finite, and the cardinality of Gn is also finite. This proof relies on a previously established result on a generalized S-unit equation and provides an explicit algorithm for finding the sets Ni and N.

A recently proposed method called an manipulability realm allows for the assessment of a robot's grasp stability in terms of human-robot distance. Nonetheless, its implementation in a shared physical space between humans and robots might present challenges due to its requirement for a minimum safe distance between human and robot. To tackle this issue, we introduce a new approach to estimate the manipulability realm while maintaining close proximity between humans and objects during two-handed conveyance. Achieving consistent hand positioning between the human and robot is essential for seamless handover, but current methods often fall short due to limitations in accuracy, performance, or the need for specialized equipment. To address these shortcomings, we propose a new technique that uses the Iterative Closest Point (ICP) algorithm to align point clouds from the human and robot end-effectors, ensuring accurate handover while maintaining safety in shared physical spaces.

A key aspect of the Standard Model is the Higgs boson's self-interaction, which can be detected at the LHC through the Higgs boson pair creation and its subsequent decay into a specific set of particles. However, the difficulties in analyzing these processes are substantial, leading to a very low signal-to-background ratio and a limited sensitivity of current LHC experiments to constrain the self-coupling constant of the Higgs boson. As a result of several recent studies, improvements in analyzing Higgs boson pair creation processes have been discovered that can significantly increase sensitivity and thus constrain the self-coupling constant. In this analysis, two of these improvements are explored in detail using a unique approach that combines the properties of the final state particles in the Higgs boson decays to increase the sensitivity of the measurement. A notable finding is that using this specific approach to filter the final state particles significantly increases sensitivity at $\sqrt{s} = 13\ \textrm{Tera}\textrm{eV}$, resulting in a self-coupling constraint roughly three times more stringent than the LHC's current limit.

Our study investigates how explorers develop an understanding of their surroundings in a complex 3D environment, specifically focusing on whether and how they learn to use their ego-centric perspective to create a stable, world-centered reference point for 感知 rotation and perception of their environment.  We designed a simple, self-updating sensory system in which the same object can be perceived from different angles as it rotates, and found that agents using only this input can successfully learn to use their ego-centric perspective as a stable reference point.  This learned stability helps the agents navigate the environment and form a coherent understanding of their surroundings, and our results suggest that simple, repetitive motion of the environment can produce distinct and recognizable perspectives that serve as the foundation for creating a stable, reliable reference point for navigation and perception.

A persistent challenge in combating COVID-19 misinformation is the task of accurately identifying users' acceptance or refusal of false information spread on social media. Our research focuses on developing automated systems to recognize verbal and written responses to COVID-19 vaccine misinformation shared on Twitter. By using a carefully constructed experimental framework, we have developed a robust dataset consisting of 4822 real-world Twitter threads featuring four types of response categories along with significant baseline models, deep learning models, and ensemble strategies. These deep learning models, which exhibit an ensemble performance F1 score of 0.7305, significantly outperform our established baseline techniques with an improvement of approximately 17%. Furthermore, our analysis reveals that the choice of feature representation, whether it be character-level, token-level, or a combination of both, greatly influences the effectiveness of deep learning models, ultimately leading to state-of-the-art performance results.

A new technique has been developed to produce isolated attosecond light pulses by intense field interaction, using a strong external field to stabilize the extreme conditions needed for their generation. A straightforward mathematical explanation based on quantum electrodynamics reveals that the external field can isolate and enhance these pulses within a tunnel ionization model. By optimizing the characteristics of both the external and intense fields, it is possible to achieve controlled pulses with durations under 150 as and energies greater than 100 fC.

We generated synthetic light curves for 20 potential companions in 13 varying configurations, incorporating distinct mass loss rates, albedos, and surface heat distributions. These models were then compared with observed light curves of Algol's fresh companions to evaluate their efficacy in reproducing the observed variable patterns. Our simulations successfully matched observed periods and amplitude patterns for 11 of these contenders, although the measured mass loss rates diverge from those predicted by standard wind models. Furthermore, the current research is limited to specific phase and amplitude combinations due to the uniform albedo and thermal properties assigned to all proposed faces of the secondary object.

This research focuses on determining the minimum L^2 norm threshold, denoted as $\theta_{\min}$, in order to guarantee a nonlinear Schrödinger equation's solution will explode given an initial condition in the free space outside of a convex barrier. It is known that the minimum L^2 norm threshold can be represented in this context as the sum of a well-defined positive constant in the convex barrier's environment and a continuously dependent operator on the barrier. A key mathematical tool in this research is the variational method, in conjunction with a nonlinear Steinhammel-type inequality.

Physically-informed neural networks (PINNs) offer an innovative solution to partial differential equations (PDEs) by integrating physical laws into a data-driven model with minimal assumptions. Although PINNs can provide global solutions without meshing and handle irregular domains effectively, they face computational issues with time-consuming gradient evaluations at dense collocation points. Research has explored adaptive node creation to mitigate this concern, and in particular, our Residual-Driven Adaptive Node creation technique (RANG) demonstrates superior performance. Using partial and fully-coupled PDEs, we evaluated RANG's efficiency, and found it significantly reduces computation time while maintaining high solution accuracy.

In this research, we simulate Ferrofettransistors (FeFETs) with multiple domains, considering the movement of domain walls and their effect on the transfer characteristic. We discovered that the presence of domain walls in a ferroelectric channel results in a dual-voltage response, exhibiting Negative Capacitance behavior. We obtained the voltage drop across the ferroelectric layer by solving the self-consistent Poisson and Landau--Ginzburg equations, demonstrating a bistable system with effective subthreshold swing improvement and threshold voltage control via domain engineering. We modeled the interaction between the channel and domain walls using a self-consistent approach that includes the distribution of domain walls near the gate and their impact on the voltage drop. We obtained the internal voltage distribution of the ferroelectric layer, indicating a dual-voltage response, with a soft voltage response at low voltages and a steeper response at higher voltages. Additionally, we simulate the movement of domain walls under an electric field, as shown in the provided image. We observed that the voltage drop across the ferroelectric layer changes significantly during the domain wall motion, exhibiting characteristics of Negative Capacitance. We verified our results by comparing our simulations with Finite Element Method (FEM) approaches, as shown in the provided image, and our calculations demonstrate excellent agreement with the FEM results.

This study deploys an Freight Ecosystem Dependency-Fragility insight graph for mapping the connections between freight functions and their effects on other modules within the ecosystem. By using a system-wide approach, this analysis offers a more comprehensive understanding of how disruptions can propagate through the freight ecosystem. Following this, an investigation into fragility diffusion was conducted using freight simulation to model the impact of disruptions under various conditions. Additionally, multiple artificial disruptions were created and assessed to gain further dependence insights, ultimately identifying key areas for strategic investment to bolster freight resilience.

This study investigates a stochastic intricate Ginzburg-Landau equation subject to pure jump disturbances, and we demonstrate that its associated Markov process is ergodic, with implications for applications in physics and mathematics.

Let G be a group and denote by $\mathcal{L}(G)$, the set of isomorphism classes of the power graphs of G. In this context, we identify power graphs of nilpotent groups with power graphs of their respective Sylow subgroups, and similarly, for the directed Laplacian graphs, we consider the directed Laplacian graphs of a p-group G and a nilpotent group G.

A high-precision detector system has been meticulously designed, utilizing advanced computer simulations to predict the impact of cosmic radiation on particle accelerators. This innovative system, highly sensitive and adaptable, can study the behavior of particles at particle accelerators and the effects of cosmic radiation on the Earth's magnetic field and moon. By accurately forecasting the movement of particles in complex environments, such as the Large Hadron Collider, researchers can understand the properties of unknown particles and their roles in the universe.

This study builds upon pre-existing vision models, adapting them for image recognition tasks regardless of the required rotation. We first examine the relationship between the natural images' rotational symmetry and the artificial neural networks' artificial periodicity. To mitigate this incompatibility, we develop novel building blocks for the model, one of which involves introducing notational elements that are equivalent under rotation, and another with a more complex convolution operation. We also propose methods for identifying and address the symmetry issue during training, either by making the model's response rotation-invariant or rotation-equivariant. We put our building blocks and techniques for learning in practice with the ImageNet dataset and observe notable enhancements in the performance of state-of-the-art image recognition models.

Geometric shape information can be effectively represented by point clouds, which offer efficient storage and simplified processing of complex shapes. Recent studies have tried to use Graph Convolutional Networks (GCNs) to tackle point cloud tasks, such as classification and segmentation. However, the success of GCNs heavily relies on the quality of the point cloud graph, which is primarily constructed using the k-nearest neighbor approach but often results in poor performance due to the irregularity of point clouds and the resulting distorted gradients. To overcome this issue, the proposed method, named Harmonic Graph Convolution, can create a high-quality point cloud graph that produces better results, specifically by creating an optimized neighbor and generating a more uniform graph through a novel convolution method. Experimentally, the proposed method has shown superior performance, with the GC model achieving approximately 3.5% higher accuracy than standard GCNs on ShapeNet classification.

Recent studies on Indirect Code Execution (IDT) assaults at the binary level have demonstrated their efficacy in bypassing code-signature and bypassing security measures, but they often suffer from the drawbacks of difficult Trojan-assault code generation, difficult payload data embedding, and difficult assault verification. In an effort to address these challenges, we introduce a novel IDT assault methodology called hostless trojan assault, which is specifically designed to overcome the limitations associated with host-assisted trojan assaults. By leveraging the features of base64 encoding and custom semantic operations, our approach is able to perform reliable and efficient hostless trojan assaults, even at the byte-level. Moreover, our hostless trojan assault method also offers advantages of automatic and efficient data embedding, support for byte-level hostless trojan assaults, and reliable assessment of hostless trojan assaults through decoupling and reverse engineering processes. Through a series of case studies, our research shows that the hostless trojan assault method outperforms the existing IDT assault methods, but it is, however, vulnerable to security threats, including security measures, security-aware code generation and obfuscation, leading to hostless trojan assault failures and system vulnerabilities.

We introduce an update on the ROSIE integral field device currently used on the Magellan IMACS spectrometer, focusing on the new setup for the 500-920 nm wavelength range. The IFU and its new camera have undergone significant testing and the device has been successfully installed in October 2021. The update also discusses the current status of the ROSIE IFU for the 380-500 nm range, which is still undergoing development, along with the proposed plan for the remaining work.

In this paper, the carbon-carbon collision system is analyzed to determine its linear and periodic orbits, which then serve as a foundation for non-abelian eikonal amplitudes for scattering and non-abelian wave functions. These elements enable the calculation of cross sections at various energies. The findings suggest that without considering specific vibrational states, the model is insufficient to accurately describe the collision at low energies. Furthermore, the model amplitudes for periodic and linear trajectories can be related to the method used in astrophysics for calculating reaction rates, which may be applied to a broader range of reaction types.

To accurately assess the potential for terrestrial planets to harbor life, as seen on Earth, it's crucial to understand the composition of their interiors. This study utilized three-dimensional radiative hydrodynamic simulations to model the core compositions of six terrestrial-type exoplanets from the Kepler mission and three hypothetical Earth-like planets. By analyzing stellar compositions, we determined the chemical and mass distributions within the core, mantle, and crust of each exoplanet through the Simulations of Core Accretion. Employing the model's results and assuming no planetary differentiation occurred during core formation, we found that most exoplanets experienced significant fractionation between their cores and crusts due to their stellar composition. By analyzing the effects of planetary mass and stellar metallicity on core silicate and iron contents, we identified which elements would be enriched or depleted in the core or crust of each exoplanet. This study also highlighted the importance of considering the actual stellar composition of each host star, rather than using the solar composition as a proxy. By applying these methods to similar planet-bearing stars, we can gain deeper insight into their core compositions and, ultimately, their potential to support life.

Our proposed system uses an attention mechanism to optimize the efficiency of wireless positioning fueled by LoRaSig. We exploit variations in channel responses across different frequencies to enhance frequency-dependent communication signals as a reliable reference for locating an device's (TAG) precise position. To manage computational complexity and focus on the most influential features of the channel response, we developed an attention mechanism that weighs their importance. Based on this mechanism, we trained a neural network for accurate wireless positioning and achieved a remarkable 87% reduction in calculation complexity compared to methods that process all frequency resources, alongside a remarkable 0.3m improvement in positioning accuracy our experiments demonstrated.

This paper proposes a comprehensive framework for the semantic interpretation of basic modal logic with intuitionistic first-order logic as its core, redefining the logical structure as a type of topological category rather than the traditional semantic method involving Kripke structures. This new approach not only provides a sound and complete modal logic but also fully characterizes the valid formulas through a semantic approach, thereby providing a stronger foundation than existing results based on first-order logic with modal extensions. This result holds true even when the logical structure is stripped down to its simplest form, consisting only of the negation and box operators, leading to a new and stronger characterization of valid formulas compared to combinations of first-order and modal logic alone.

A bipartite graph's edges can be colored individually to reflect the colors of adjacent vertices. The minimum such required edge coloring is known as the edge chromatic index, denoted χ'_b(G). In bipartite graphs with no isolated vertices, the edge coloring is always at least the graph's maximum vertex degree, and it is considered robust if this minimum is equal to that maximum degree. In particular, bipartite graphs with the property of being edge-1-factorizable have a minimum robust edge coloring that equals their maximum degree. A conjecture proposed that bipartite graphs with certain symmetry and connectivity would have a robust edge coloring that equals their maximum degree. However, this conjecture has been shown to be inaccurate through a counterexample.

In the author's joint research with Lev Borisov and Evgeny Shmatov, it was determined that on the Levenshtein graph of the Hamming space, any function that is both harmonic and non-zero must have a minimal number of support points at least $\sqrt{m}$, where $m$ represents the order of the graph's Laplacian. For the specific case of $m=O(\log n)$, the lower bound of the support is reduced to a constant. This research provides the optimal lower bound of the support on the Hamming graph of the $n$-dimensional vector space over a 3-element field for specific eigenvalue intervals, where the support size at least equals $\sqrt{m-1}$. This result generalizes the Levenshtein graph finding, as it is a specific instance of the Hamming graph, and also is complemented by an associated expansion theorem.

COPASI, a widely-used computational tool for biochemical modeling, offers various analysis methods but falls short when users need to create custom, script-based investigations. A recent enhancement, ShinyCOPASI, addresses this limitation by providing an easy-to-use web interface for developing and executing intricate model explorations with a CBCS server, featuring a pre-built library of ServerResource classes for seamless model access and analysis result display.

One of the significant hurdles for Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning models to overcome is their potential to conflate cause and effect, making it difficult to accurately interpret their decisions. To resolve this challenge, researchers have increasingly turned to explainable AI, which aims to clarify how and why a model reaches a certain conclusion. Among the techniques used to analyze and resolve ambiguity in AI models are specific methods and metrics, though there is limited understanding of how these methods perform in practice. To address this knowledge gap, this research paper outlines a comprehensive framework consisting of three key components: a set of evaluation tasks, a collection of datasets, and three specific use cases. By employing various algorithms on datasets that adhere to these evaluation tasks and comparing the results across the different use cases, the study identifies, explains, and quantifies the uncertainties present in existing AI methods, ultimately aiding in the development of more trustworthy and interpretable AI systems.

We examine a specific von Neumann algebra formed from a compact quantum group, derived from a subgroup and its associated category functions. The central question is whether this function von Neumann algebra equals the von Neumann algebra of central functions. We establish that it is always包含, with equality holding in the case of a quasi-Hopf algebra. However, in the context of Hopf algebras, equality occurs if and only if the category of modules for a subgroup satisfies the property of being a Calabi-Yau odd category. Furthermore, in the case of a compact matrix quantum group and a subgroup that is also a compact matrix quantum group, equality occurs if and and only the quantum dimension of any object in the category of modules has a specific value equal to 1.

This strategy iteration employs an imprecise GMRES method to externally estimate a linear system of very large marked stochastic dynamic programming problems. Stochastic dynamic programming, a widely used statistical prediction and decision analysis tool, has found marked applications in modeling and optimization of numerous complex systems. However, for systems of extremely large dimensions, traditional strategy iteration and synchronous policy evaluation methods using power iteration are inefficient due to their slow convergence rates. To address this, a research strategy involving partitioning and block iterative solving of the linear system is proposed. By introducing an imprecise general minimum residual method and developing a corresponding strategy iteration, convergence is achieved, as illustrated on a test case of very large marked stochastic dynamic programming problem.

In a significant result, Herzog, Hibi, and Popescu established the Gorensteinness of the canonical module for the edge ideal of a weighted directed graph, deriving the depth of the total quotient ring as a consequence. We recover their theorem under the specific condition of a single outgoing edge for each vertex, also obtaining a comparable result for the ideal generated by the powers of edges originating from a vertex of a weighted directed graph where each edge has a weight of one.

This paper examines an inverse problem of estimating a computer simulation's input from its output, where the data are generated values of computer models over time and follow an unknown, dependent pattern influenced by a single factor. To achieve this, we suggest an efficient method called Multiple Contour Assessment, which uses the Theorem of Conserved Quantities to identify the maximum likelihood estimate of a computer model's input parameter from time series data. The MCA algorithm is robust and straightforward to implement as it doesn't rely on specific model characteristics, and only requires determining the median of the data, for which we extend an iterative algorithm from real to time series values, along with an efficient alternative approach for high-dimensional simulations. In our experiments, the MCA method is tested on various scenarios, including when the data are smooth and has noise, as well as in complex, non-smooth scenarios, and compares its results to those of existing methods that are applicable to these situations.

This study examines resilient learning in regional data environments through the lens of Q-learning, comparing it to distributed learning and showing that it can be seen as a form of implicit cooperation between agents in adjacent regions. By analyzing the stability of this approach, we develop conditions that guarantee safe region transitions and a cooperative protocol based on these conditions. Experimental results demonstrate that this resilient learning method outperforms fully decentralized agents and certain distributed learning methods, while being more efficient than approaches that rely on cloud support.

The reconstruction of jets in high-energy collisions is crucial for understanding the properties of the quark-gluon plasma. To isolate the effects of the medium on jet fragmentation, researchers often combine jets with a tagged isolated photon. This study investigates the changes in jet fragmentation in Pb-Pb collisions by comparing measurements to those in proton-proton collisions at the same energy energy. By analyzing the distribution of the cumulative sum of charged-particle fragmentation particles in a cone around the jet axis, and normalizing it by the total number of charged particles in the event, scientists can isolate the effects of the medium on jet fragmentation. This analysis, based on data collected by the CMS experiment at the LHC, reveals that jets interacting with the quark-gluon plasma tend to break down into smaller, more numerous fragments. This phenomenon is supported by both theoretical and other experimental models.

Recent research has provided compelling evidence that infinite series resembling Apéry numbers can determine the values of colored non-alternating multiple zeta expressions with weight values, particularly in a recent discovery by the third author which extended previous work by the second and third authors for m=1, particularly in relation to an identity by Brown and a theorem by Apéry. The purpose of this paper is to generalize the identity by Brown by providing two new infinite series representations under specific conditions related to non-negative integer parameters. These new identities will ultimately reveal multiple relationships between these infinite series, the values of colored non-alternating multiple zeta expressions with mixed parity, and the values of key constants including π and ln2.

Recent research has confirmed that the brown dwarf binary WISEA J153429.75-104303.3, also known as "The Mishap", has a primary component with a mass of 53 MJ and a secondary component with a mass of 35 MJ. Both objects are young, with an estimated age of 12 million years, and are part of the ρ Ophiuchus star cluster. Using new data, we have re-evaluated the properties of this brown dwarf binary, including its mass, radius, and temperature, and compared them to theoretical models. We also calculated the convective zone depths of both objects, finding that they are consistent with recent predictions. This research contributes to our understanding of the formation and evolution of low-mass binary systems, and provides new constraints on the age and mass of the system.

Our study examines the production of various particles including pions, kaons, protons, and $\phi$ mesons in Xe-Xe collisions at the CERN Heavy Ion Collider at a speed of $\sqrt{s_{\rm NN}} = 5.44$ TeV per nucleon pair using the CAZ detector. The measured rapidity density of these particles in the central region is compared with other measurements taken at lower energies and with theoretical models. The spherically symmetric distribution of these particles on a plane perpendicular to the beam axis shows no significant difference between the collision types. We have developed a novel, data-driven approach to extrapolate and extend parton distribution functions (PDFs) within the context of proton and neutron, beyond the regions covered by experimental data. This approach is compatible with any PDF parameterization model or reweighting technique. Our method involves extending the x-boson (x_B) range from 0 to 1 by incorporating two distinct x_B extremes, thereby yielding a continuous and physically relevant PDF even in x_B regions inaccessible through experiment. Our approach utilizes the PDFs provided by the CT10 parameterization as a baseline and supplements them with the PDF modification imparted by the photon-flavored octet sea (PFES) proposed by Adelman and Tassie. x_B sea (x_B <~ 0.00043). Our findings suggest that PFES contributes to the proton's mineral content in x_B <~ 0.00043.

Producing building blocks directly from local soil on Mars and the Moon using in-situ construction techniques is a key goal for future planetary colonization and infrastructure development. To test the in-situ construction method in which heat is applied to regolith to create bonds in formed parts, a study on the in-situ formation of materials from Martian, lunar, and Earth-based sand was conducted. This involved subjecting the materials to different temperatures for various durations to observe their properties and understand the underlying formation process. Research found that the materials' chemical composition and mineral content significantly affect their physical properties when formed at high temperatures. Specifically, the optimal forming temperature for the materials varied, and the resulting mechanical attributes of each material were significantly influenced by the Sintering heat. For example, the compressive strength of forming materials made from Martian and lunar sand increased by 400% and 300%, respectively, when the Sintering heat was set to 900°C for 90 minutes. In contrast, the compressive strength of forming materials made from quartz and silica sand set at 900°C showed little to no improvement and in some cases even decreased, indicating that the Sintering heat has a significant impact on the material's properties and performance potential.

The Rayleigh-Plateau instability of a liquid layer on a fiber is investigated with consideration of both static and dynamic conditions. 
A theoretical model incorporating liquid viscosity, evaporation, and interaction between the liquid and the supporting fiber is developed. 
This model is capable of describing the slip between the liquid and the fiber, while offering additional flexibility through two free parameters. 
To obtain the dispersion relations, a matched asymptotic expansion is employed across the liquid-air interface, the contact line, and the air-liquid-meniscus triangle. 
Two new non-dimensional numbers are introduced to better understand the system, and the results are further supported by extensive numerical simulations.

We analyze the spectral energy distributions of a sample of nearby star-forming galaxies to assess Star Formation Rates derived from different tracers. The effect of assuming submillimeter continuum emission is dominated by dust rather than dust being affected by external radiation sources. When the external radiation temperature is taken into account, this additional energy contributes minimally to submillimeter emission. However, incorporating this external radiation is crucial for accurately modeling infrared and submillimeter fluxes, particularly in cases where there is significant ultraviolet and far-infrared external radiation. For a sample of nearby star-forming galaxies, SFRs estimated from the Brackett-17 alpha line and submillimeter emission are consistent, with a ratio of 0.91. However, when comparing the rest-frame 2 micron to submillimeter emission as indicators of SFR, we find the former systematically overestimates submillimeter-based SFR by a factor of 1.9.

This paper is the initial part of a two-part study that delves into the B-type quantum subgroup of $\mathfrak{sl}_{2n}$, denoted as $D_{n+1}$. The subsection explores the key symmetries of a specific type of representation, known as regional, which is a component of the $\mathfrak{sl}_{n}$ algebra and contains a component of the $D_{n+1}$ algebra and a finite sum of $\mathfrak{sl}_{n}$ representations. The authors develop a method to construct an action of the Hecke algebra $H_{n+1}$ on these regional and symmetry algebras, allowing them to assign algebra labels to these components. The paper also establishes a correspondence between this algebra and the $(n+1)$-ary braid algebra, making it possible to establish a relationship with the A-type quantum subgroup of $\mathfrak{sl}_{2n+1}$. The section concludes by outlining some open questions for future investigation.

The goal of diffusion models is to develop a singular generative model capable of producing high-quality samples across diverse domains. Achieving this objective requires resolving two primary challenges: sampling from the distribution of each individual domain and ensuring a seamless transition between domains. Our novel approach adresses these issues by employing a unified framework for both inter-domain translation and domain separation. By transforming domain-specific distributions into a latent space, we leverage this representation to facilitate domain traversal and control the diffusion process for accurate sample generation within each domain. Our method has demonstrated efficacy in facilitating inter-domain translation and producing high-quality samples from various domains with minimal computational overhead, requiring only a two-stage training regimen.

This research introduces an innovative approach to recognizing mathematical expressions, leveraging data generated by motion sensors to overcomes limitations of handwritten input from users. To achieve this, an annotation system was developed to collect structured information from the 401 participants who wrote mathematical expressions while wearing a device with four motion sensors. Subsequently, a Convolutional Neural Network was employed to process and analyze the sensor data, which was then integrated with user identity information through a Transformer-based model specifically trained to recognize handwritten mathematical expressions. Moreover, a method known as Attention Summation was devised to aggregate the attention maps from multiple modalities, including both human and student inputs, in order to enhance the overall input representation and improve recognition performance.

To create more authentic spoken interviews, it is necessary to simulate not only speech content but also their lengths.  Traditionally, speech lengths are modeled using statistical methods, but these methods require substantial computational resources and can be sensitive to minor changes in speech patterns.  To overcome this, researchers have developed a non-statistical approach to simulate speech lengths based on a median-based system.  This method uses cut speech segments, filling gaps with noise, and determines the total length of each simulated speech by comparing it to a distribution of real speech lengths.  Although non-statistical in nature, this median-driven system can be efficiently implemented even on basic hardware and is resilient to changes in speech pattern distributions.  To validate its effectiveness, the study simulated speech lengths of three distinct speakers on three different hardware devices, showcasing its speed advantages over traditional statistical methods.

To and from presence-absence data, integrated single-species, multi-species, and integrated models can be estimated using Bayesian methods with the spHabitat R package. This package facilitates parameter and predictive uncertainty assessment as well as species distribution predictions. By combining integrated modeling, data reduction, and correlation structure, the package improves computational efficiency, resulting in packages like sphabitat, sphabitatDS, and sphabitatM. These models take into account species' ecological requirements, correlations, and random effects. Furthermore, the package enables detection of spatial patterns in random effects data.

This paper showcases the Skincare initiative, an interactive learning system that aids healthcare professionals and patients in the differentiation between various types of benign and malignant skin lesions. Benign skin lesions, characterized by non-aggressive and localized properties, are distinct from malignant lesions such as Basal Cell Carcinoma, Squamous Cell Carcinoma, Melanoma, and Kerkatinocytoma, which have aggressive features and the potential to spread. The Skincare initiative employs a comprehensive database of over 100,000 images, each annotated with a diagnosis and associated text, to train deep learning models for automatic interaction and diagnosis of skin lesions through the analysis of visual features, lesion description, and associated tags.

To enhance the accuracy of cosmological redshift estimates, we have developed an optimized Autoencoder (EA) that processes Type Ia supernovae spectra. By treating each spectrum as a separate time frame in four distinct filter bands, EA can now analyze the entire Type Ia supernovae dataset. Our EA, being a novel deep learning technique, incorporates intrinsic stochasticity to better capture correlations among supernovae spectra. As a result, EA significantly reduces estimation bias and randomly selects the most suitable reference supernovae for each new spectrum. Building on this approach, we have made our EA estimation process non-iterative, significantly decreasing processing time. EA's results have surpassed those of traditional machine learning algorithms in terms of consistency and efficiency, ultimately enabling more accurate estimates of cosmological redshifts with an unprecedented precision of 0.0004.

High-resolution near-infrared integral field spectroscopy of the galaxy GLASS J1010+5616 at z=2.09 reveals detailed information about its dust formation. The data is derived from the use of the VLT/MUSE instrument with significant lensing (d=3.6) to resolve its spatial distribution across 0.35-1.05 kpc. The integration of its H2 emission lines shows its spatial coincidence with the continuum and [OIII] regions, suggesting the presence of a dense and extended star-forming region. This finding is further supported by the presence of a 1.65+/-0.36 kpc long, 0.45+/-0.15 kpc wide structure in its H2 map which is consistent with its 2D [OIII] and continuum data. This structure is likely a result of gravitational lensing effects as supported by the detection of multiple magnification peaks within its 2D [OIII] data. This suggests the presence of multiple gravitational lensing features within its interior components to the 0.35 kpc scale. This study showcases how H2 detection in rest-frame mid-IR via the H2 S(1) line provides a complementary view of star formation in high-redshift galaxies to [OIII], helping to resolve their spatial and physical properties to understand star formation efficiency.

The growth of turbulent plumes is significantly hindered by the presence of solid particles, resulting in complex dynamics that are challenging to replicate in laboratory settings. The differences between model turbulence (isotropy, no particles) and real-life situation (turbulence with particles) are quite substantial, leading to a lack of understanding of turbulent plume behavior in solid-particle-filled environments. To investigate this problem, a laboratory-scale turbulent plume was developed using a tank with an upward turbulent jet and a suspended particle load, accompanied by a corresponding theoretical model. The effects of varying particle properties and concentrations on plume behavior were studied through a combination of experimental observations and simulations. The effects of particles on turbulent plume dynamics are primarily attributed to two factors: increased stress due to particle interactions and a theoretical increase in viscosity, leading to altered stress-to-convective-buoyancy ratio and turbulence intensity in the plume.

Understanding the spread of epidemics in networks and hypergraphs over time has led to various theoretical conclusions. 
In this study, we establish conditions under which certain network and epidemic models will lead to the complete eradication of an infection, 
utilizing the properties of a set of eigenvalues and eigenvectors. 
We demonstrate that as the number of connections increases in a specific type of hypergraph model, the resulting extinction behavior closely mirrors that of a standard Susceptible-Infected epidemiological model. 
We also develop methods to estimate the time it takes for an infection to die out and propose several methods for assessing the accuracy of these estimations.
Our findings have significant implications for predicting the natural extinction of infections and assessing the reliability of estimates derived from the SI-model.

Recent studies of the van der Waal ferromagnet, CrI$_3$, have revealed that it exhibits not only ferromagnetic order but also antiferromagnetic coupling between layers. In a CrI$_3$ bilayer, a transition from ferromagnetic order to a spin-canted state can be triggered by a structural distortion caused by an in-plane force, simulating a constraint imposed by a substrate. This constraint induces a non-zero in-plane asymmetry in the research's simulation methods, thereby activating the in-plane asymmetry of the spin structure. As a result, the spins within a triangle exhibit a Rashba-associated influence, where they adopt an arrangement characterized by in-plane asymmetry, distinct from a pattern that is symmetric with respect to chirality.

Standard solar-type dynamos are incapable of producing magnetic cycles in slowly rotating stars due to their reliance on rapid rotation for the Coriolis force's influence on convection-zone dynamics. However, researchers have proposed that slowly rotating stars with significant surface differential rotation might still exhibit magnetic cycles. In this study, we utilized MHD simulations to investigate the development of magnetic cycles in slowly rotating stars with enhanced surface differential rotation, expecting their magnetic cycle behavior to be similar to rapidly rotating stars. Our experiments involved modifying the surface differential rotation in a standard solar-type dynamo model until magnetic cycles persisted, even in slowly rotating stars. The results showed that a specific range of surface differential rotation could support the development of magnetic cycles, primarily driven by the interaction between shear instabilities and the Coriolis force's influence on convective-zone inflow, in a process known as the Taylor-Proudman effect. The proposed optimal surface differential rotation range may hold implications for understanding the dynamo of certain types of stars, such as mid-A main-sequence stars and specific subdwarf B stars with mid-field magnetic fields.

Deep learning models are highly sensitive to the quality of their underlying representations, which in turn affects their overall performance. To address the limitations of traditional supervised learning in dealing with diverse, complex data formats, our proposed deep framework utilizes multiple input channels from various modalities to automatically build robust representations that enhance multiple task performances. At its core is a k-fan multimodal deep framework consisting of multiple functional branches, each responsible for a distinct task, united by a shared representation space produced through a central aggregation module called the Deep Framework Aggregator. This module combines input modalities into a unified space where Task-Independent Representation, free of modality-specific noise, and Task-Specific Representation, free of irrelevance to each respective task, are extracted through dedicated Task Extraction Modules. Our deep framework has been successfully applied to two major classification tasks: currency detection and semantic segmentation, showcasing significant improvements in performance over state-of-the-art models.

This paper presents a model checker based on DPOR that allows for highly customizable 
adjustments in order to efficiently verify single-threaded programs with multiple threads. 
In our implementation, McMini significantly reduces model-checking overhead for a specific 
subset of C programs with single data-race issues or those lacking such problems when using 
a specific memory-visibility model. To achieve this reduction, McMini employs several techniques 
including the use of an optimized DPOR, a method to limit the exploration of threads with no data-races, 
a technique that avoids rechecking data-races found previously, and an algorithm based on integer 
linear programming to fix data-races. The model-checking results of various data-race scenarios 
using McMini are presented in a comprehensive study that also reveals the impact of different 
configurations on its performance.

In an effort to curb the rapid spread of false information, WhatsApp recently implemented a feature limiting message sharing, requiring users to display the starting point of the message, including their profile picture and the text, in the shared content. Given that these details can reveal sensitive personal information, we examine the impact of such a restriction on misinformation dissemination by modeling both WhatsApp-based and non-WhatsApp-based misinformation campaigns. Our game-theoretic analysis shows that the WhatsApp sharing restriction significantly decreases the spread of false information, but incentivizes the unintentional dissemination of personal data. Furthermore, our numerical simulations suggest that the frequency of forwardings cannot solely account for the effectiveness of an misinformation campaign, and that the WhatsApp sharing restriction leads to a noticeable decrease in the propagation of false information, alongside a significant increase in the voluntary sharing of personal information.

A theoretical framework is developed to assess the genetic prevalence spectrum in a large population from a branching process, where a sample is drawn and rare alleles are identified within it. The theoretical findings are validated through simulations, and the results are compared with those obtained from a standard Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium model for a population of a given size.

This paper presents an innovative system designed to detect voice spoofing attempts within a single, integrated framework. The proposed system employs a dual-module structure: a primary deep learning-based spoofing counteraction network and a supplementary anomaly detection module that focuses on attention to flag unexpected voice samples as potential fakes. The prominent modules within the integrated framework are an inter-spectrogram correlation network and a vocal tract identifier network, both of which generate new features for effective spoofing detection. The modular anomaly detection module utilizes a generator and a discriminator network to identify voice samples that deviate from the expected patterns within the integrated framework's training data. An additional module detecting abnormal attention patterns serves as a final safeguard against spoofing attacks. Used on the VCS18 framework and VCS18+ADM framework formed by adding the anomaly detection module to the primary framework, both were extensively tested on the AM-Speaker dataset, revealing that the integrated system significantly enhanced spoofing detection rates and that R-F1 performance continued to improve with the addition of the attention detection module.

In certain types of supersymmetric cosmological models, supergravity is generally too complex to be practical, except for a specific class of supersymmetric inflaton models where the complex supergravity Lagrangian can be simplified into a much more manageable form, allowing for comprehensive analytical and numerical analysis of various cosmological parameters during and after inflation.

When associated with specific control wavelengths, signal and idler photons are identically distributed across all other directions of the spectrum independent of signal to idler intensity ratios. However, this equality does not hold for the pairs of photons associated with each other, showing a distinct difference in wavelength between signal and idler photons. This difference is observed both experimentally and through theoretical calculations, showing that the wavelength difference is approximately equal to the linewidth of the pump laser.

Our investigation of empty and quantum-filled coplanar microwave resonators utilizes terahertz spectroscopy of near-field electromagnetic responses. By employing a phase-resolved, scanning terahertz microscopes with a 10 ps resolution and ~5 µm spatial resolution, we map out the phase and amplitude of the resonator's fundamental transverse electromagnetic mode. Our phase-scans align with numerical simulations, providing a precise description of the mode's spatial distribution. Notably, our experiments also quantify energy loss processes in the resonator, confirming that near-field interactions with environment do not contribute to loss at temperatures of 300 mK or lower, thus validating the purity of quantum bits built upon microwave resonators.

We establish the following results for partitioning the real line into multiple subsets: (1) Under certain conditions related to cardinals, it's proven that for any regular cardinal $\kappa$ with a specific property, the real line can be divided into $\kappa$ many Divisible sets of type 1, where each set consists of sets with specific measure and category properties. (2) Similarly, it's proven that the real line can be partitioned into $\kappa$ many sets, where each set contains a subset of type 1 with measure zero and category zero properties, based on $\kappa$'s property related to cofinality and additivity of measures. (3) It's also proven that for cardinals, the real line can be divided into two sets, each containing a subset with specific measure and category properties, both having specific properties related to cardinality and initial order. (4) Finally, it's proven that for cardinals, the real line can be partitioned into $\aleph_2$ many sets, where each set contains a subset with specific measure and category properties, involving additivity of measures and stationary sets.

In light of the persistent challenge of reliably investing in alternative assets like private equity and real estate, agent-based models have emerged as a valuable tool for analyzing these complex investments. This paper delves into the underlying mechanics of ABM that influence their results, using a simple example to illustrate the model's components. Specifically, it examines the impact of an novel investment approach on the model's outcomes, aiming to explain, rather than merely report, the findings. Our investigation reveals the underlying relationships between key model factors, offering insights into the importance of initial conditions and how they shape the model's dynamics. This analysis agent-based model outcomes, aiming to illustrate the impact of an novel investment approach on the model's results, offering a deeper understanding of the underlying relationships between key model factors, including the importance of initial conditions and how they shape the model's dynamics.

This research proposes a straightforward yet effective method for automatically identifying and classifying network attack traffic, presenting a challenge to current techniques that rely on predefined signature-based systems and machine learning approaches, which often struggle with the growing diversity of attack methods and false positives respectively. Our proposed solution leverages an in-depth analysis of protocol handshakes, utilizing a series of statistical measures to identify attack patterns, and encompasses more than 50 prominent attack types including those that are signatureless, encompassing tools like Masquerade attacks and Teardrop attacks. To demonstrate the proposed method's efficacy, we used a 10Gb test environment to evaluate its performance in distinguishing attack traffic from legitimate user activity, and found that our approach accurately identifies 96% of attack packets while maintaining a low rate of errors. In contrast, we found that a comparable system based on the open-source Scapy tool suite and a machine learning algorithm based on TCP flags achieved lower accuracy rates of 60%.

Gapping of magnons occurs through their coupling with electronic substrates, and in superconducting environments, this coupling inherits the gap parameter via exchange interaction, resulting in a hybrid gap that simultaneously affects both magnons and electrons. We demonstrate that the interplay between superconductivity and magnetism gives rise to a novel phenomenon in which the gap parameter's effect on magnons can be effectively controlled or "gated". This "magnon gating" effect stems from the presence of time-reversal symmetry-breaking in the superconductor and allows us to achieve the isolation of pure magnetic responses at very high frequencies, potentially in the range of terahertz.

A prominent challenge in federated learning is adapting to new categories that emerge at client devices. This research introduces a pioneering approach for training deep models across a network of client devices, incorporating novel categories. Unlike existing methods, our method training happens simultaneously on devices with established and new categories. We examine how effective our method is on diverse datasets, comparing it to other approaches in terms of performance and efficiency.

There has been significant interest in entangled Greenberger-Horne-Zeilinger states across various fields, such as quantum information and foundational studies. However, there is a limited set of verification methods available, with most being suitable only for lower-dimensional systems. A new, comprehensive and efficient state evaluation method for arbitrary dimensional Greenberger-Horne-Zeilinger states is proposed in this paper. The suggested method involves determining specific probabilities of measuring maximal correlations using generalized Bell inequalities and prepares the necessary quantum state of pure entanglement. The analysis reveals that it is both possible and practical to prepare high-dimensional Greenberger-Horne-Zeilinger states while meeting the requirements of a detailed state evaluation, surpassing existing approaches and enabling the detailed investigation of higher dimensional entangled states.

This paper focuses on small-dimensional MISO systems supported by intelligent reflecting surfaces and develops low-complexity active beamforming strategies under both active and passive transmission modes. All reflectant nodes are assumed to utilize single-element antennas and share a single IRS. To minimize the overall transmit power in the system, the authors formulate an optimization problem involving active and reflective beamforming. Since this problem is non-convex, the proposed solution utilizes a two-step cascaded estimation approach combined with alternative optimization techniques. Furthermore, the paper presents an alternative passive beamforming strategy based on fractional programming. Finally, the results from simulations confirm the effectiveness of the proposed methods in improving system performance.

This research examines how U.S. regional news outlets responded to the U.S. COVID pandemic between March 2020 and March 2021, analyzing changes in coverage, intensity, and user engagement. Utilizing a large dataset of news articles and official pandemic statistics, we investigated correlations and causality between media reports and COVID-related metrics such as infections and deaths, as well as outlet ratings. Findings show a unit root in both publication volume and intensity post-pandemic onset, with no self-correlation in volumes and an positive autocorrelation in intensity that diminishes over time. Contrasting with prior studies on national media, we found that news intensity displays autocorrelation in our dataset. While COVID mortality exhibited time-reverse Granger causality with both volume and intensity, indicating a media reaction to local fatalities, no similar effect was observed for infection rates. During the pandemic, a disparity emerged among regional outlets, with variations in user engagement and user diversity among top and bottom perfoming outlets.

This research explores the learning and progression of basic counting skills by artificial neural networks, specifically those modified to mimic the basic structure of biological brains. The study employed three types of neural networks: one enhanced to recall past inputs, another to predict past outputs, and two standard models for comparison. The results indicate that adjusting the network to incorporate memory of its previous outputs allows it to learn complex counting patterns that standard models struggled to master, such as the sequence of odd numbers. Notably, this ability to recall past data also enables the network to accurately predict the progression of a pattern after it has been disrupted. These findings shed light on how neural networks can learn sequential tasks and the conditions under which they can perform complex mathematical operations.

A variation of a Bloom filter called a xored Bloom filter utilizes bitstrings to represent and store a collection of data items, leveraging bitstring operations to prevent false positives in the presence of duplicates. A more advanced version, the xor filter, adopts a cactus graph structure of bitstrings to optimize this process. While the xored Bloom filter has shown significant potential in reducing errors, especially with duplicates, it has not fully addressed spatial complexity and query time concerns. Consequently, several adaptations and extensions of the xored Bloom filter have been proposed to deal with these limitations, but they have not maintained an optimal balance. A theoretical analysis was conducted to evaluate the performance of various n-stage xored Bloom filters with bitstrings of varying lengths, and it was found that an optimal configuration exists under specific conditions. This optimal setup can be identified through the solution of a non-linear optimization problem that can be efficiently resolved in constant time. As a result, an efficient and memory-optimized cactus graph representation of a Bloom filter can be achieved under specific conditions, essentially providing an improved version of the cuckoo filter. This improved structure, the xor filter, maintains similar query efficiency to the cuckoo filter while offering significant space and time savings over traditional Bloom and xored Bloom filters when dealing with duplicates. Construction of the xor filter can also be executed efficiently in expected linear time.

This paper's core goal is to establish connections between various inconclusive results in the realm of homogeneous bodies with specific properties along various cross-sections. A central theorem of the paper relates the above mentioned sections to a connection between support functions and a type of function known as subharmonic functions.

This study proposes a ground-up methodology for forecasting market trends, based on a temporal sequence of market actions, incorporating their respective expenses and share volumes. A Hidden Markov Model is leveraged to create a trend classifier that categorizes market trends, which is subsequently used in combination with a K-Nearest Neighbors classifier to provide market progress predictions, identifying the direction of market movement. This predictive capability is supplemented by anomaly detection in market costs to flag atypical patterns, which may signify shifts in market trends. This approach was tested on the NASDAQ 100 index, with a focus on the most heavily traded stock - Apple Inc. - revealing insights into the optimal entry and exit points for a proposed investment strategy, which incorporates a 2.5% minimum profit and an 8.0% maximum loss threshold.

Federated learning offers a privacy-preserving method for distributed machine learning, relying on the principle of information theoretic security by ensuring that server messages contain negligible information about client data. Unfortunately, current federated learning techniques are vulnerable to manipulation through adversarial data sent by clients or biased server messages, which can compromise privacy. This issue is exacerbated in scenarios where data and model information are asymmetric, as currently assumed in federated learning. To address this challenge, we introduce FLVoogd, a federated learning protocol that preserves privacy in both client and server components. Drawing inspiration from the secret sharing protocol developed by Voogd et al., our approach transforms models and model updates into secret polynomials, utilizing a efficient change-basis to facilitate efficiency. This results in a more cost-effective solution compared to existing alternative federated learning methods.

This study examines a common challenge in autonomous vehicle development, namely, simulating realistic driving environments to refine complex navigation systems. We simulate a home-like setting with movable objects to increase the realism of simulated data for training navigation models. To bridge the gap between simulated and real-world data, we fine-tune image processing parameters to enhance the realism of simulated images, thereby improving their fidelity to real-world data. The simulated platform utilizes Gazebo for environment simulation and a simulated robot version of the Figure 8 figure-hugging platform for agent modeling and training. The results indicate that image manipulation techniques can effectively mitigate the Sim2Real divide by making simulated images more realistic. Furthermore, we trained and fine-tuned navigation models on simulated data and tested them on real robot data, achieving strong performance, including image similarity metrics, policy robustness, and navigation accuracy metrics of 0.892 for image similarity, 0.85 for robustness, and 0.90 for navigation accuracy.

Our research introduces a content-agnostic deepfake creation approach, which generates content-agnostic strong deepfakes from a single reference image of a person and arbitrary target images, maintaining high fidelity across various scenarios and environments. To counteract deepfake creation, we develop identification models capable of detecting deepfakes in a wide range of content and settings. However, deepfake creation becomes infeasible when trained on the generated deepfakes due to the complex mapping problems. Therefore, we employ neural network guided model transfer to transfer the features extracted from deepfake creation model to the features encoded by a pre-trained VGG-NET to train the deepfake identification models. We evaluate the proposed approach on the deepfake detection challenge dataset, and demonstrate that the content-agnostic strong deepfakes cannot be distinguished from real images on the chosen challenge dataset, when using the deepfake creation model's feature extractor. Furthermore, we show that the chosen pre-trained VGG-NET's feature extractor can be used to train the deepfake identifier to identify deepfakes on the chosen challenge dataset.

The discovery of sub-Neptunian exoplanets spanning various mass ranges has piqued interest in understanding their diverse atmospheric compositions, particularly those with masses similar to HD 63444 b.  Employing atmospheric modeling, we investigate whether the characteristics of HD 63444 b can be attributed to an inflated gas envelope or a concealed ocean.  By applying a equation of state that integrates solubility equilibrium, we develop a predictive framework for both possibilities.  In contrast, traditional ideal gas equations may lead to underestimating envelope inflation for warm gas giants, particularly those with hydrogen-dominated atmospheres.  Our research highlights that for HD 63444 b, the distinction between a concealed ocean and an oceanless atmosphere becomes negligible if its atmospheric composition is metal-rich, regardless of the equation of state used.  However, if its atmosphere is hydrogen-dominated, a sub-photospheric ocean is favored if its radius is larger than 0.94 times the radius of Jupiter, or smaller than 0.90 times the radius of Jupiter, leaving intermediate radii ambiguous.  In general, a transit radius alone may not definitively distinguish between an ocean-dominated atmosphere and a fully mixed gas giant atmosphere, emphasizing the significance of diverse atmospheric radii measurements, especially those obtained through phase-resolved phase curves or secondary eclipsases, to resolve this compositional ambiguity.

Achieving pattern classification in complex domains, such as medical diagnosis, relies heavily on the capabilities of deep learning architectures, particularly those of artificial neural networks. Despite the deep understanding of their artificial counterparts, the simulation of equivalent computational power in the human brain remains a significant mystery. Recent advancements in spiking neural networks, thanks to the Theoretical Biological Pattern Separation Theorem, have made a significant stride towards resolving this mystery by providing a solid foundation for further research. In this paper, we take the first major step in closing the gap between these mathematical proofs and their practical application by developing the fully spiking Backpropagation algorithm. Our algorithm's innovative design simulates the brain's learning process more accurately than existing alternatives, achieving these similarities through unsupervised learning for intra-layer connections and sparse, layer-by-layer supervised learning for weights. Our results demonstrate the effectiveness of the SPIN algorithm through extensive experiments across multiple datasets, showcasing its superiority in terms of efficiency and performance.

This report, a contribution to NLPOG 2021, is a compilation of the French Natural Language Processing group's findings from the 15th Text+Speech Language Understanding Competition's Out-of-Lexicon challenge.  Composed primarily of novel words and phrases not included in the language's standard vocabulary, the language data used in the competition presents an especially difficult challenge.  The report describes each participant team, their respective approach to the problem, and is accompanied by the associated submission files for the competition.

This study presents a novel approach combining an adaptive generalized polynomial chaos expansion with an optimal test-based a posteriori error assessment for approximating functions within a specific domain that includes random factors. This approach is verified under the assumption that the function can be represented by a series of Hermite polynomials and is posteriorly verified using an optimal test based on the Cauchy-Schwartz inequality. This study draws inspiration from a prior approach, but differs in that the corresponding integral is not a probability but a specific value within a defined domain. This method enables the assessment of the efficiency of GC expansions, both in terms of their ability to capture a function and the optimality of their basis. This approach is demonstrated through three examples involving the smooth function y = (1 + x^2)^-1 on a continuous d-dimensional domain and two functions containing the random factor ξ with d = 1 and singularities on distinct domains.

This paper introduces an innovative technique for detecting and isolating changes in a changing system where not all data points are available. The method utilizes adaptive statistical tests to identify alterations and a sequential algorithm to detect when these changes occur. Once an alteration is identified, the method uses an optimal information-theoretic approach to determine the best system component to adjust for the missing data and employs a verification process to ensure the accuracy of the conclusion. Initially, the paper outlines a framework for handling partial observations and demonstrates the effectiveness of the approach through theoretical proofs and practical experiments on a ChipMultiplexer system.

We analyze the formation of satellite dwarf galaxies through the combined effects of tidal disruption and accretion cycles, as well as their influence on the Milky Way's halo. To explore this, we utilize a self-gravitating N-body simulation that incorporates tidal forces, along with hydrodynamics and particle injection methods to model accretion. Furthermore, we develop an artificial tagging system to distinguish particles subject to different processes, allowing us to study the dynamics of these dwarf galaxies. To further understand the galaxy evolution, we apply a self-consistent isochrone fitting technique to the simulated stellar populations. Our results indicate that all explored satellite dwarf galaxies underwent significant accretion and mass loss events, resulting in their present-day configuration. This process is characterized by multiple star formation bursts, affecting the chemical composition and evolution of these galaxies. Ultimately, their present-day configuration is a result of successive mass loss and accretion events. This study provides the theoretical foundation for understanding the evolution of satellite dwarf galaxies through the analysis of their chemical composition and evolution.

Advanced document extraction frameworks, capable of visually rich document understanding, have reached a level of maturity that allows for seamless integration of natural language processing and computer vision techniques. Nonetheless, their widespread adoption is hindered by two main challenges: the difficulty in accurately label-rich data due to its complex visual layout and lack of available, annotation-free pre-trained models for visually based document elements. To address these gaps, this paper presents two innovations: the first is a novel approach to automate the labeling process for rich document visuals using computer vision, while the second is the development of a set of pre-trained image-based models for element type and connection line detection to minimize the required labeled data needed to fine-tune their performance on specific tasks. Through thorough experimentation and evaluation of various document extraction tasks, this paper showcases the proposed approaches can substantially lower the expense associated with labeling costs and enhance the overall performance of document extraction frameworks.

Our study of EuS/InAs heterostructures reveals that the magnetic and spin-orbit interactions within InAs are induced by the proximity effect from EuS even at the EuS monolayer, corresponding to a 0.5 nm thickness. Using MFM, we observed an unusual, non-monotonically decreasing interface magnetic thickness with a 1 nm saturation point. X-ray analysis enabled us to examine the EuS/InAs linkage configuration's impact on the electronic structure at the heterostructure interface. We applied a hybrid electronic arrangement model that incorporates both a localized magnetic moment and a spin-split InAs interface state with a 0.4 eV magnitude bandgap. It is concluded that the InAs interface state origin prefers a 3D character over 2D. Additionally, the magnetic properties within InAs are highly sensitive to the EuS monolayer and linkage configuration, with the spin-orbit coupling in InAs always exhibiting a larger magnitude than the exchange interaction.

A detailed examination of the real number line and its power set reveals an interesting pattern of Borel wadge classes, which can be grouped into distinct, equivalence-like categories based on a specific relationship. Although it's known that these classes, when restricted to certain types of sets, can be fully described arithmetically, a major breakthrough shows that all classes, whether analytic or not, follow a consistent pattern of a specific type, and similarly, they all share properties related to a higher-type mathematical operation.

Deep neural networks (DNNs) have demonstrated remarkable potential for deployment in resource-constrained environments, primarily through model compression techniques such as model pruning. However, conventional pruning techniques have several drawbacks, including the need for post-pruning model quantization, which can be time-consuming and inaccurate. Our research introduces ClickTrain, a fine-detailed architecture-preserving pruning technique that overcomes these limitations. ClickTrain employs fine-detailed architecture-preserving pruning and pre/post-training quantization for model compression, ensuring that the pruned model maintains high performance without requiring additional processing. We developed ClickTrain's fine-detailed architecture-preserving pruning technique, which preserves the network's original structure and ensures that the pruned model maintains high performance. Our research also introduces VPB and L2-Norm-based pruning techniques, along with an innovative fine-detailed architecture-preserving pruning technique called ReWeighted Layer Compression (RLC). We evaluated ClickTrain on various deep neural networks and achieved superior performance compared to state-of-the-art pruning methods, including a 10.71% and 14.18% higher pruning rate and lower compression rate, respectively. ClickTrain achieved a 2.70x higher pruning rate and 1.41x better accuracy compared to the competing method on ResNet-50, and a 1.63x and 1.27x higher pruning rate compared to the competing method on MobileNetV2 and ShuffleNetV2.
